stem: Isolated jaundice in neonate 5 days old all other exam normal ( doctor notice yellow skin in pediatric clinic , parents came for postpartum checkup ) What is the diagnosis?
key_concept:
Neonatal jaundice by timing and examination.
  • First 24 hours = pathological (haemolysis) until proven otherwise
  • Days 2 to 3, well baby = physiological
  • First week with poor intake = breastfeeding jaundice
  • End of week 1 into weeks 2 to 3, thriving breastfed baby, normal exam = breast milk jaundice (observe, continue breastfeeding)
  • Beyond 2 weeks or conjugated bilirubin or pale stools = investigate (biliary atresia)
  • Neurological signs + very high bilirubin = kernicterus
exam_pearl: A normal neurological exam excludes kernicterus; jaundice only becomes kernicterus when the baby shows neuro signs.

stem: 55 y/o Women with birad 0 The mammogram show overlaps shadows bilaterally what to do:
OptD: some surgical or biopsy for both breasts
why_right: BI-RADS 0 means the mammogram is incomplete: findings such as overlapping shadows cannot be categorised without more imaging. The correct action is further investigation (additional diagnostic mammographic views such as spot compression, and/or ultrasound), then assigning a final BI-RADS category.
why_wrong_block:
A. Short-interval (6-month) follow-up is for BI-RADS 3, probably benign; a BI-RADS 0 study has no final category yet.
B. Routine yearly or screening-interval mammography is for BI-RADS 1 or 2 (negative or benign).
D. Biopsy is for BI-RADS 4 or 5 lesions; overlapping tissue shadows do not justify bilateral tissue sampling before work-up is complete.
key_concept:
BI-RADS actions:
  • 0: incomplete, additional imaging
  • 1 to 2: negative or benign, routine screening
  • 3: probably benign, short-interval follow-up (about 6 months)
  • 4 to 5: suspicious or highly suggestive, core needle biopsy
  • 6: known malignancy, treat
exam_pearl: BI-RADS 0 is not a result; it is a request for more imaging.

stem: Patient after MVA has severe back pain, exam is normal, respiration is normal Neurosurgical consult is ordered What measures is best now
key_concept:
Suspected spinal injury: protect first, then image.
  • High energy mechanism + midline back or neck pain = assume spinal injury.
  • Maintain immobilization (log roll, collar) until cleared.
  • CT is the imaging of choice to clear the spine.
  • MRI if neurological deficit or suspected cord or ligament injury.
  • A normal neuro exam does not exclude an unstable fracture.
exam_pearl: "Best measure now" in a stable patient awaiting a consult points to protection (immobilization); "best test" points to CT.

stem: Elderly pt~ 70y/o after elective orthopedic surgery was in icu when he wakes up was alert but confused asking "where I'm?" And trying to remove the canula, what to do:
OptC: keep assuring him and adequate lighting
why_right: An elderly patient waking in ICU after surgery who is alert but "confused", disoriented ("where am I?") and pulling at the cannula has postoperative delirium. First line management is non pharmacological: reorientation and reassurance, adequate lighting, glasses and hearing aids, presence of family, normal sleep wake cycle, plus searching for and correcting the cause. Drugs are kept for distress or danger that does not settle with these measures.
why_wrong_block:
A. Haloperidol: low dose short term use is right when agitation is severe and dangerous to the patient or staff despite non drug measures; not as the first step.
B. Quetiapine: an antipsychotic alternative when one is needed, preferred in Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia where haloperidol worsens symptoms; still second line after non drug care.
key_concept:
Delirium: treat the cause and start with non drug measures.
  • Reorient, reassure, family presence, clock and calendar
  • Good lighting by day, dark and quiet at night, glasses and hearing aids
  • Look for cause: infection, drugs, pain, retention, hypoxia, electrolytes
  • Severe dangerous agitation: low dose haloperidol, short term
  • Avoid benzodiazepines unless alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal
exam_pearl: Pulling at lines alone does not justify sedation; only harm that persists after non drug measures does.

stem: Elderly with UTI and suspected urosepsis admitted 2 days later he developed acute confusion with fluctuations in awareness, he was AGITATED what to do??

Delirium = acute onset, fluctuating attention and awareness, usually from a medical cause.
  • Treat the cause (here the UTI and sepsis)
  • Non drug measures first: sleep cycle, reorientation, lighting, aids, family
  • Antipsychotic only for dangerous agitation
  • Avoid restraint and benzodiazepines
exam_pearl: "Agitated" tempts you to sedate, but exams reward non drug measures plus treating the cause unless there is danger.

stem: 21 year old patient with right iliac fossa pain for 7 days on examination: palpable mass at the iliac fossa WBC high US done showing appendiceal mass with Collection What to do:
why_right: Pain for 7 days with a palpable RIF mass means the appendix has already been walled off (an appendiceal mass, here with a collection). Operating early in this setting is hazardous because of dense inflammatory adhesions, so the first line is non-operative care: IV antibiotics, fluids and close monitoring, with appendectomy deferred. This recall's key is non interventional management because it is the only option that avoids immediate surgery.
why_wrong_block:
B. Laparoscopic appendectomy is for acute uncomplicated appendicitis presenting early; with a 7 day history and a formed mass, operating risks bowel injury and fistula.
C. Open appendectomy has the same problem as laparoscopy in a late presentation with a mass; it is not the first step for an appendiceal mass or abscess.
D. Exploratory laparotomy is for generalized peritonitis or an unstable patient; this patient has a localized mass.
key_concept:
Late appendicitis with a mass is treated non-operatively first.
  • Early uncomplicated appendicitis: laparoscopic appendectomy.
  • Phlegmon (mass, no collection): IV antibiotics, conservative.
  • Abscess (collection): percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics, then interval appendectomy.
  • Small collection: antibiotics alone may suffice.
  • Generalized peritonitis or instability: operate.
  • Older patient after recovery: colonoscopy to exclude malignancy.
exam_pearl: Days of pain plus a palpable mass flips the answer away from appendectomy toward non-operative care.

stem: Man with inguinal hernia with mild pain
why_right: An inguinal hernia causing mild pain is symptomatic, so it should be repaired. Tension-free mesh repair (open mesh, e.g. Lichtenstein, for a primary unilateral hernia) is the standard because it has the lowest recurrence.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bassini is a tissue (suture) repair under tension with higher recurrence than mesh; it is reserved for when mesh cannot be used, such as a contaminated field.
C. Watchful waiting suits a painless (asymptomatic) hernia in a man who prefers to avoid surgery; this hernia already causes pain, so elective repair is advised.
key_concept:
Symptomatic inguinal hernia = elective mesh repair.
  • Primary unilateral: open mesh repair.
  • Bilateral or recurrent: laparoscopic mesh repair.
  • Faster recovery needed: laparoscopic.
  • Strangulated or large complex hernia: open repair.
  • Tissue repair (Bassini, Shouldice) only if mesh is not suitable.
exam_pearl: Recurrent or bilateral flips the answer from open mesh to laparoscopic mesh.

stem: splenic laceration grade3 : whats management :
key_concept:
Splenic injury: stability decides, not the grade.
  • Stable: non-operative management with monitoring.
  • Stable with contrast blush: angioembolization.
  • Unstable or peritonitis: splenectomy (laparotomy).
  • Failure of observation (falling Hb, instability): operate.
  • After splenectomy: vaccinate against encapsulated organisms.
exam_pearl: Any hypotension that does not respond to fluids flips the answer from observation to laparotomy, whatever the grade.

stem: A 36-year-old man was stabbed in the right lower quadrant of his abdomen 1 hour back. He complained of pain at the wound site. Local wound exploration revealed penetration of the anterior abdominal fascia. Blood pressure 110/62 mmHg Heart rate 87 /min Temperature 37.2 °C Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: stabbed in the right lower quadrant
penetration of the anterior abdominal fascia
why_right: The patient is hemodynamically stable (BP 110/62, HR 87, afebrile) after a stab wound, and the only finding is anterior fascial penetration on local exploration. Fascial breach alone is not a laparotomy indication, so a stable abdominal trauma patient is evaluated with CT abdomen to look for peritoneal violation and organ injury.
why_wrong_block:
B. Observation alone ignores a known fascial breach; serial exams can be part of care, but the next step here is to define the injury with CT.
C. Diagnostic laparoscopy is invasive; it is used when CT is equivocal or to look for diaphragmatic or peritoneal injury, not as the first step in a stable patient.
D. Exploratory laparotomy is for instability, peritonitis, evisceration, omentum in the wound, or positive CT findings, none of which are present.
key_concept:
Penetrating abdominal trauma: stability decides.
  • Stable: CT abdomen.
  • Unstable stab wound: laparotomy.
  • Peritonitis, evisceration, omentum in wound: laparotomy.
  • Unstable blunt trauma: FAST; positive leads to laparotomy.
  • Positive CT findings: laparotomy.
exam_pearl: Add hypotension, peritonitis or evisceration and the answer flips to laparotomy.

stem: Elderly diabetic, black toe, dorsalis absent/not palpable, next or initial management:
why_right: An elderly diabetic with a black toe (gangrene) and an absent dorsalis pedis pulse has suspected critical limb ischemia. The first investigation is the ankle brachial index, a bedside non-invasive test that confirms and grades arterial disease before duplex, CT angiography and revascularization planning.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tissue biopsy is for a chronic non-healing ulcer suspected of malignant change; gangrene from ischemia is diagnosed by vascular assessment, not histology.
C. MRI is for suspected osteomyelitis under a diabetic foot ulcer; it does not assess arterial perfusion, which is the issue with a black toe and absent pulse.
key_concept:
Ischemic foot work-up ladder.
  • Step 1: ABI.
  • Step 2: arterial duplex ultrasound.
  • Step 3: CT angiography to plan revascularization.
  • Calcified vessels in diabetes can falsely raise ABI; use toe pressures if so.
  • Probe to bone or suspected osteomyelitis: X ray then MRI.
exam_pearl: A falsely high or normal ABI in a diabetic with absent pulses means calcified arteries, not a normal circulation.

stem: What's would decrease if patient loss 25% of their blood volume
why_right: Losing 25% of blood volume is class II hemorrhage (15 to 30%). In class II, compensatory vasoconstriction keeps systolic BP normal but raises diastolic pressure, so the pulse pressure narrows; it is the first pressure parameter to fall.
why_wrong_block:
B. Urine output in class II is only mildly reduced and still close to normal; it falls clearly in class III and IV, so it is not the most expected change.
C. GCS is preserved in class II (mild anxiety only); confusion and lethargy appear in class III and IV.
D. Heart rate rises (tachycardia) with blood loss; it does not decrease.
key_concept:
Hemorrhagic shock classes by % volume lost.
  • I (up to 15%): near normal vitals.
  • II (15 to 30%): tachycardia, narrowed pulse pressure, systolic BP normal.
  • III (30 to 40%): systolic BP falls, confusion, low urine output.
  • IV (over 40%): marked hypotension, negligible urine, lethargy.
exam_pearl: Systolic BP first drops in class III; if the loss is 30 to 40% the expected answer becomes hypotension.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot version: A trauma patient who lost 25% of his blood volume. Which of the following is most expected to be decreased? A. Urine output B. Pulse pressure C. Respiratory rate D. Glasco coma scale. Answer: B (Pulse pressure).

stem: Testicular torsion full symptoms & exam & U/S Clinical picture The Q asking for Tx
OptB: detwist the testicle + If pain relief discharge
why_right: The stem gives the full clinical picture plus exam and U/S of testicular torsion and asks for treatment. Torsion is a surgical emergency: the definitive management is urgent scrotal exploration with detorsion and orchiopexy (fixing the contralateral testis too), ideally within about 6 hours of pain onset to save the testis.
why_wrong_block: B. Detwist the testicle and discharge if pain relief: manual detorsion is only a temporizing bedside manoeuvre while theatre is arranged; pain relief does not guarantee full untwisting, and the patient still needs surgical exploration and bilateral fixation, never discharge.
key_concept:
Suspected testicular torsion = surgery, not imaging or observation.
  • Picture: sudden severe pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex
  • Doppler only if the diagnosis is uncertain (absent flow); never delay theatre for it
  • Treatment: scrotal exploration + detorsion + bilateral orchiopexy
  • Torsion of appendage (blue dot, upper pole pain): conservative with NSAIDs
  • Epididymo-orchitis (increased flow): antibiotics + analgesia
exam_pearl: Manual detorsion with relief of pain still ends in the operating room; a discharge option in a torsion stem is always the trap.

stem: Trauma patient with hypotension, X-Ray reveled: Trachea shifted to the right, expanded lungs and widened mediastinum. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: A trauma patient with hypotension and a widened mediastinum has a traumatic aortic injury until proven otherwise. The mediastinal hematoma pushes the trachea to the right, a classic X-ray sign of aortic rupture, while expanded lungs rule out a large hemothorax or pneumothorax as the cause. Confirm with CT angiography if the patient can be stabilized.
why_wrong_block:
A. Massive hemothorax: would show a whited-out hemithorax with dull percussion and a collapsed lung, not expanded lungs with an isolated wide mediastinum.
B. Pneumothorax: shows absent lung markings and a collapsed lung; the lungs here are expanded. A tension pneumothorax would shift the trachea away from a hyperresonant side, not widen the mediastinum.
D. Spontaneous pneumothorax: by definition occurs without trauma (typically a tall thin smoker with a ruptured bleb) and would not explain the widened mediastinum.
key_concept:
Blunt chest trauma + widened mediastinum = aortic injury.
  • Other X-ray clues: tracheal or NG tube deviation to the right, loss of aortic knob, apical cap, left hemothorax
  • Stable: CT angiography; unstable: bedside echo (TEE)
  • Tension pneumothorax: hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, trachea away, raised JVP
  • Massive hemothorax: dullness, collapsed lung, more than 1500 ml on chest tube = thoracotomy
exam_pearl: Expanded lungs on the X-ray remove both pneumothorax and hemothorax; what is left with a wide mediastinum is the aorta.

stem: Pt post lap chole, next morning developed productive cough + high temperature Most appropriate next step?
why_right: Fever with a productive cough on the next morning after surgery (postoperative day 1) is classically due to atelectasis: post-anaesthesia hypoventilation and splinting from upper abdominal port pain cause retained secretions and alveolar collapse. Treatment is to re-expand the lung with chest physiotherapy, incentive spirometry, early mobilisation and adequate analgesia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observation: the collapse will not resolve without active lung expansion and can progress to pneumonia, so doing nothing is wrong.
B. CT scan: not needed for day 1 fever with a chest picture; CT is for suspected intra-abdominal collection, leak or abscess, which typically appear later (around day 5 onward).
C. Sputum culture: fits a postoperative pneumonia, which usually appears from about day 3 with consolidation; on day 1 the cause is atelectasis, not infection.
key_concept:
Postoperative fever by timing (the classic 'W' ladder).
  • Day 1-2: atelectasis (Wind) = chest physiotherapy, incentive spirometry
  • Day 3-5: pneumonia, UTI (Water), phlebitis
  • Day 5-7: wound infection, anastomotic leak
  • Day 7+: DVT/PE, deep abscess (CT)
  • Very early (hours): malignant hyperthermia, transfusion reaction, necrotizing infection
exam_pearl: Same symptoms, different day: fever and cough on day 1 = atelectasis (physio); on day 3-5 = pneumonia (cultures, antibiotics).

stem: A 26-year-old woman presented with insomnia, fatigue, and sadness. She delivered her first child 5 days ago. Examination reveals a tearful and depressed appearance. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: delivered her first child 5 days ago
why_right: This recall's key reads the "tearful and depressed appearance" with insomnia, fatigue and sadness after her first delivery as postpartum depression, so it is treated rather than watched. An SSRI (sertraline is preferred, as it is compatible with breastfeeding) is the first line drug treatment, combined with psychological support.
why_wrong_block:
B. Benzodiazepines do not treat depression, cause sedation and dependence, and pass into breast milk; they are not a treatment for postpartum mood disorders.
C. Follow-up in 1 week is the plan for postpartum blues (mild, transient low mood starting around days 3 to 5 and resolving within 2 weeks); the key treats this presentation as depression needing treatment, so watchful waiting alone is not chosen.
D. Multivitamins have no role in treating postpartum mood symptoms.
key_concept:
Postpartum mood spectrum: decide by timing, duration and severity.
  • Blues: days 3 to 5, resolves within 2 weeks = reassure, follow up
  • Depression: symptoms beyond 2 weeks or severe = SSRI (sertraline) plus psychotherapy
  • Psychosis: first 2 weeks, hallucinations, delusions, confusion = admit, antipsychotic
  • Any thoughts of harm to self or baby = urgent psychiatry
exam_pearl: Mild, transient low mood in the first 2 weeks = blues (reassure, follow up); a depressive picture needing treatment = SSRI, sertraline if breastfeeding.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed recall: Postpartum pt *5 days* Looked depressed what to give: ssri / multivitamins (no highlight). Screenshot (Q0252): Answer: A.

stem: A diabetic pt has ulcer in lateral foot with discharge and granulation but intact pulse
why_right: This recall's key is venous ulcer, following the rule ulcer + intact pulse = venous (absent pulse = arterial), with a granulating, discharging base that fits the moist, pink base of a venous ulcer. On this teaching, the diabetes is a distractor once the pulses are confirmed present.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ischemic: arterial ulcers have absent or weak pulses, a punched-out painful ulcer with a pale, sloughy or necrotic base, not healthy granulation; the pulses here are intact.
C. Malignant: suspect a Marjolin (squamous cell) change in a long-standing non-healing ulcer with rolled everted edges, rapid growth or bleeding; biopsy then. Nothing here suggests it.
D. Neuropathic: the classic diabetic foot ulcer, painless over pressure points (metatarsal heads, heel, lateral border over the 5th metatarsal) with intact pulses and reduced sensation; the strongest competing answer for a diabetic foot.
key_concept:
Leg/foot ulcer approach: feel the pulses first.
  • Absent pulse: arterial ulcer, punched out, painful, necrotic base: arterial Doppler
  • Intact pulse + gaiter area, pigmentation, edema, granulating base: venous: venous duplex
  • Intact pulse + diabetic, pressure point, painless, callus, loss of sensation: neuropathic
  • Chronic non-healing with rolled edge: biopsy for Marjolin ulcer
exam_pearl: Site decides between venous and neuropathic: medial malleolus/gaiter area = venous; plantar or pressure areas of a diabetic foot = neuropathic.

stem: female had head injury presenting with to ED with GCS 8/15, with dark ecchymosis around the eyes and crusted blood in her nose nostril. What is the best way to secure her airway?
highlight_terms_source: crusted blood in her nose nostril
why_right: GCS 8 is an indication for a definitive airway. Dark ecchymosis around the eyes (raccoon eyes) and blood in the nostrils point to a basilar skull fracture, which contraindicates anything passed through the nose. So the airway is secured by orotracheal intubation (rapid sequence, with in-line cervical spine stabilization).
why_wrong_block:
B. Nasotracheal intubation: contraindicated with a suspected base of skull fracture (raccoon eyes, nasal bleeding, CSF rhinorrhea) because the tube can pass through the cribriform plate into the cranium; it is also a blind technique.
C. Cricothyroidotomy: the surgical rescue airway when oral intubation fails or is impossible, for example severe maxillofacial or mandibular injury with profuse oral bleeding; the mouth route here is usable.
D. Tracheostomy: a slow, elective or semi-elective procedure for prolonged ventilation or upper airway obstruction, not the emergency airway in the trauma bay.
key_concept:
Trauma airway: intubate for GCS ≤8, SpO2 <88%, unconsciousness or aspiration risk; then choose the route.
  • Default: orotracheal intubation with C-spine protection
  • Basilar skull fracture (raccoon eyes, Battle sign, CSF leak, hemotympanum): avoid nasal tubes
  • Severe facial/mandibular injury or failed intubation: cricothyroidotomy
  • Tracheostomy: not an emergency trauma airway
exam_pearl: Raccoon eyes do not push you to a surgical airway; they only forbid the nose. Facial bone destruction is what pushes you to cricothyroidotomy.

stem: A 10-days old boy presents in the ER after circumcision with 5-hours of bleeding from the operation site, what is the best step to do? Had high PTT
OptA: Applying pressure on the operation site
why_right: A 10-day-old with 5 hours of oozing after circumcision is actively bleeding, so the immediate best step is local hemostasis: firm direct pressure on the operation site. The "high PTT" points to an underlying coagulopathy (hemophilia, or vitamin K deficiency bleeding if vitamin K was missed), which is then worked up and corrected, but bleeding control with pressure comes first.
why_wrong_block:
B. Surgical exploration of the wound is for bleeding that persists despite pressure with a normal coagulation profile (a surgical vessel); with a prolonged PTT, operating before correcting the coagulopathy worsens bleeding.
C. The recall did not preserve this option's text; if it was factor replacement, vitamin K or FFP, that is the correction that follows once pressure is applied and the cause is identified.
D. Reassurance is unsafe: 5 hours of continuous bleeding in a neonate with a prolonged PTT is a true bleeding disorder until proven otherwise.
key_concept:
Post-circumcision bleeding in a neonate:
  • Step 1: direct pressure (local hemostasis)
  • Check PT, PTT, platelets; give vitamin K if not received
  • Isolated prolonged PTT in a boy: hemophilia A or B, give the specific factor
  • PT and PTT both prolonged: common pathway or vitamin K deficiency
  • Persistent bleeding with normal coagulation: surgical exploration
exam_pearl: Circumcision bleeding in a boy with high PTT is a classic first sign of hemophilia; pressure first, then factor.

stem: A 40 to 45 year-old man undergoes colonoscopy, which reveals a polyp in the colon. Histopathologic examination shows a tubular adenoma measuring 1.5 cm in size. During the procedure, the surgeon remove 1.3 cm of the lesion. When should the next colonoscopy screening be performed?
why_right: The decisive clue is that the polyp measured 1.5 cm but the surgeon removed only 1.3 cm of it: the resection was incomplete and residual adenoma is left behind. Incomplete or piecemeal removal of a large adenoma needs an early repeat colonoscopy within a few months (3-6 months) to clear the site, before any routine surveillance interval applies.
why_wrong_block:
B. Every 3 years: the correct interval for a completely removed tubular adenoma ≥10 mm (an advanced adenoma); it does not apply while residual polyp remains.
C. Every 5 years: matches screening with CT colonography or flexible sigmoidoscopy, or older intervals for small adenomas; too long for a partly removed large adenoma.
D. No screening needed: an adenoma is a precancerous lesion; a 40-45 year old with residual adenoma needs completion and surveillance.
key_concept:
After polypectomy: first ask whether removal was complete, then size, number and histology.
  • 1-2 tubular adenomas <10 mm: 7-10 years
  • Adenoma ≥10 mm, villous features or high-grade dysplasia: 3 years
  • Piecemeal or incomplete removal of a large polyp: short interval re-look (about 6 months)
  • Small hyperplastic polyps or normal colonoscopy (average risk): 10 years
  • Stopping surveillance is a decision for old age or limited life expectancy, not a young adult with an adenoma
exam_pearl: Read the sizes: lesion size larger than the resected size means incomplete removal, which flips 3 years into a short-interval re-look.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1825).

Surveillance interval = completeness + histology + size + number.

  • Piecemeal or incomplete removal of a large polyp: short interval re-look (about 6 months)
  • Small hyperplastic polyps or normal colonoscopy (average risk): 10 years
  • Stopping surveillance is a decision for old age or limited life expectancy, not a young adult with an adenoma

stem: A patient presented with infrequent anal bleeding did a colonoscopy that revealed one polyp size 1.5cm and a biopsy showed tubular adenoma 1.2 cm. Interval of colonoscopy?
why_right: This recall's key is 6 months. It reads the stem as a 1.5 cm polyp whose specimen measured only 1.2 cm (and was described as a biopsy), meaning the adenoma was not fully removed; residual or piecemeal-resected large adenomas are rechecked early, at about 6 months, to confirm complete clearance.
why_wrong_block:
A. No need: a tubular adenoma is precancerous and a patient with one needs surveillance; no follow up is never right here.
C. 3 years: the interval for a completely removed tubular adenoma ≥10 mm; it would be the answer if the whole polyp had been taken out in one piece.
D. 5-10 years: fits 1-2 small (<10 mm) completely removed tubular adenomas or average-risk screening, not a 1.2-1.5 cm adenoma.
key_concept:
After polypectomy: complete or not first, then size and histology.
  • 1-2 tubular adenomas <10 mm: 7-10 years
  • Adenoma ≥10 mm, villous features or high-grade dysplasia: 3 years
  • Piecemeal or incomplete removal of a large polyp: short interval re-look (about 6 months)
  • Small hyperplastic polyps or normal colonoscopy (average risk): 10 years
  • Stopping surveillance is a decision for old age or limited life expectancy, not a young adult with an adenoma
exam_pearl: If the polyp was completely removed, a 1.2-1.5 cm tubular adenoma is 3 years; the short interval only applies when tissue was left behind.

stem: A 42 year patient came with mild PR bleeding, there is no history of anything, no DM, no HTN. Colonoscopy show: 1.5 cm polyp sigmoid. Histopathology: tubular adenoma (also described as benign-looking). Which of the following true about the follow up of endoscopy?

stem: 52 year old male medically free came to the clinic complaining of red urine for 2 days associated with right flank pain, no dysuria no fever no other symptoms. On examination: right flank tenderness and palpable rectal prostate (written like this). Urine culture: negative. Urine analysis: + erythrocyte, Nitrate: absent, WBC: absent. What is the most appropriate next investigation:
why_right: Red urine with right flank pain and loin tenderness, with no dysuria, no fever, negative culture and no pyuria or nitrites, points to a ureteric or renal stone rather than infection. The first line imaging for suspected urolithiasis is a non contrast CT KUB, which detects almost all stones and also shows other renal causes of hematuria.
why_wrong_block:
A. Urine cytology: an adjunct when urothelial cancer is suspected (painless gross hematuria in an older smoker); it has low sensitivity and is not the first test for painful hematuria with flank pain.
C. Retrograde urethrogram: used after pelvic trauma with blood at the meatus or suspected urethral injury, before passing a catheter; there is no trauma here.
D. Cystoscopy: evaluates the bladder in painless gross hematuria or when bladder pathology is suspected; flank pain directs the first test to the upper tract with CT.
key_concept:
Hematuria: let the pain and the context pick the first test.
  • Painful hematuria + flank/loin pain, no infection: non contrast CT KUB (stone)
  • Fever, dysuria, pyuria/nitrites: urinalysis and culture (UTI/pyelonephritis)
  • Painless gross hematuria, older, smoker: CT urography + cystoscopy (urothelial cancer)
  • Pelvic trauma + blood at meatus: retrograde urethrogram
  • Pregnancy or child with suspected stone: ultrasound first
exam_pearl: Remove the flank pain and make it painless hematuria in a smoker, and the answer becomes cystoscopy with CT urography.

stem: 12-year-old patient presents with a 4-hour history of right sided lower abdominal pain. Examination confirms a slightly elevated, tender right testis. The lie of the testis is horizontal with no redness or edema of the scrotum. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

A. Oral analgesics: pain relief alone wastes the salvage window while the testis infarcts; analgesia (NSAID) is the treatment for torsion of a testicular appendage with a blue dot sign and normal lie.
B. Oral antibiotics: treat epididymo-orchitis, which is more gradual with fever, dysuria and scrotal redness and swelling; this scrotum has no redness or edema.

key_concept:
Acute scrotum: decide by onset, lie and redness.

  • Torsion of appendage: upper pole tenderness, blue dot sign, normal vertical lie: NSAID, conservative
  • Epididymo-orchitis: gradual, fever/dysuria, red swollen scrotum, Doppler increased flow: antibiotics
  • Idiopathic scrotal edema: painless bilateral redness extending to the groins
  • Salvage is best within about 6 hours of onset
exam_pearl: Torsion can present as lower abdominal pain in a boy; always examine the scrotum, and do not let a Doppler delay the theatre.

stem: Severe left lower leg pain for 6 hours. When examined there's no pulse. What's source of thrombus?
why_right: Severe leg pain for 6 hours with no pulse is acute limb ischemia, and an acute occlusion like this is classically embolic. Most peripheral emboli are cardiac in origin, and the commonest single source is a thrombus in the left atrium (especially the left atrial appendage) due to atrial fibrillation, so the left atrium is the expected source when no other history is given.
why_wrong_block:
B. Left ventricle: a mural thrombus forms after a recent MI or with a ventricular aneurysm or dilated cardiomyopathy; it becomes the answer only when the stem mentions a recent MI.
C. Thoracic aorta: atheromatous plaque or aneurysm can shed emboli, but this is a much less common source than the heart.
D. Abdominal aorta: an aneurysm's mural thrombus can embolize distally (often small emboli to the toes), but it is an uncommon source compared with a cardiac thrombus.
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia: embolus vs thrombosis.
  • Embolus: sudden onset, no prior claudication, often AF or recent MI, normal contralateral pulses
  • Embolic source: heart first (left atrium in AF most common; left ventricle after MI)
  • Thrombosis: on known atherosclerosis, prior claudication, more gradual onset
  • Same cardiac embolic sources cause acute mesenteric ischemia
  • 6 P's: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia
exam_pearl: Add "MI 2 weeks ago" to the stem and the source becomes the left ventricular mural thrombus.

stem: Patient just got in MVA. He responded to 500ml saline. Complains of lower abdominal pain (pelvic region). No external bleeding. FAST is positive for free fluid in abdomen. Now he is stable. What's the best INITIAL investigation now?

stem: A man presented with trauma to his chest complains of severe pain in his chest, he has severe tenderness on the chest with multiple bruises. During initial assessment the airways are patent and clear, he is alert and conscious but his chest wall is unstable when he moves or tries to take a deep breath and bruising in his right chest. Air sounds present bilaterally clear. Vital signs normal apart from saturation 86%. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: A chest wall that is unstable when he breathes, with multiple bruises and severe tenderness, describes a flail chest (multiple rib fractures with paradoxical movement). The airway is patent, he is alert, breath sounds are clear bilaterally and vitals are otherwise normal, so treatment is supportive: oxygen and adequate IV analgesia, which lets him breathe deeply and cough and often corrects the hypoxemia caused by splinting and the underlying lung contusion.
why_wrong_block:
B. Mechanical ventilation: reserved for flail chest with respiratory failure that persists despite oxygen and good analgesia, exhaustion or a falling conscious level; this patient is alert and protecting his airway.
C. Chest tube: for a pneumothorax or hemothorax; breath sounds are present and clear on both sides, so there is no pleural collection to drain.
D. Emergency thoracotomy: for massive hemothorax (about 1500 mL on insertion or 200 to 300 mL per hour), traumatic arrest or decompensation after stabilization; none applies.
key_concept:
Flail chest: treat the pain and the contused lung, not the ribs.
  • Definition: multiple adjacent ribs broken in more than one place, paradoxical movement
  • First line: oxygen + strong analgesia (IV opioids, regional or epidural block) + chest physiotherapy
  • Ventilate only if respiratory failure persists or the patient tires
  • Avoid fluid overload because of the underlying pulmonary contusion
  • Chest tube only if pneumothorax/hemothorax; thoracotomy only for massive bleeding
exam_pearl: Add drowsiness, exhaustion or worsening hypoxia despite analgesia and oxygen, and the answer becomes intubation and ventilation.

stem: 24-year-old male presents with RLQ pain and fever, diagnosed with acute appendicitis and was taken to OR for appendectomy using a Gridiron (McBurney's) incision. During surgery, the surgeon found a normal appendix. What is the appropriate action?
OptB: Resect the appendix and close the abdomen
why_right: A normal appendix found at operation for presumed appendicitis means the real cause of the RLQ pain and fever is still in the abdomen. The surgeon must not simply close: the standard move is to search for an alternative pathology through the same incision, and in a young male the classic one to exclude is an inflamed Meckel's diverticulum, found by running the terminal ileum (about 2 feet / 60 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve). Other things checked are mesenteric nodes (mesenteric adenitis), the terminal ileum (Crohn's) and, in females, the adnexa.

A. Closing without exploring leaves the true source of fever and RLQ pain (e.g., Meckel's diverticulitis, ileitis) untreated and missed.
B. Removing the normal appendix is commonly done as well, but only after the abdomen has been examined for another cause; removing it and closing at once skips the key step this question tests.
D. Conversion to a midline laparotomy is reserved for pathology that cannot be reached or managed through the gridiron incision (e.g., generalized peritonitis, perforated viscus elsewhere); it is not the first move for a normal appendix.

Normal appendix at appendectomy: explore for another cause before closing.
  • Run the terminal ileum: Meckel's diverticulitis, Crohn's ileitis
  • Look at mesentery: mesenteric adenitis
  • Females: check ovaries and tubes (ruptured cyst, torsion, PID, ectopic)
  • Normal appendix is usually removed too, to avoid future diagnostic confusion
  • Extend or convert the incision only if the found pathology demands it
exam_pearl: Meckel's rule of 2s: about 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, so run the terminal ileum before closing on a normal appendix.

stem: 10 or 12 y child on bicycle was hit by a car, what is the best confirmation to consciousness?
OptD: Signs of truma on the head
why_right: After head trauma (child hit by a car on a bicycle), the standardized, reproducible measure of level of consciousness is the Glasgow Coma Scale. It combines eye opening (1 to 4), verbal response (1 to 5) and motor response (1 to 6) into a total of 3 to 15, and serial scores track deterioration. A pediatric verbal scale is used in young children, but at 10 to 12 years the standard GCS applies.
why_wrong_block:
B. Orientation to time, place and person is only one item of the GCS (verbal 5); on its own it does not grade eye or motor response and cannot quantify a depressed level.
C. Being able to describe the accident tests memory (absence of amnesia), not a graded level of consciousness; useful in concussion history but not the confirmation tool.
D. Visible head trauma shows mechanism and injury, not the patient's level of consciousness; serious brain injury can occur with no external signs.
key_concept:
Level of consciousness in trauma = GCS (E4 V5 M6, range 3 to 15).
  • Eye: 4 spontaneous, 3 to speech, 2 to pain, 1 none
  • Verbal: 5 oriented, 4 confused, 3 inappropriate words, 2 sounds, 1 none
  • Motor: 6 obeys, 5 localizes, 4 withdraws, 3 abnormal flexion, 2 extension, 1 none
  • GCS ≤ 8: secure the airway (intubate)
  • Quick primary-survey alternative: AVPU
exam_pearl: Orientation is a GCS component, not a substitute for it; the question asks for the whole graded tool.

stem: Patient with jaundice, dark urine, pale stool and weight loss. found to have hugely distended gall bladder. High bilirubin. Elevated liver enzymes. GGT 213. Ca 19- 9 502. What is the cause?
OptB: Carcinoma of the head of the pancrease
highlight_terms_source: jaundice, dark urine, pale stool and weight loss
why_right: Painless-type obstructive jaundice (dark urine, pale stool) with weight loss, a hugely distended gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) and a very high CA19-9 indicates a malignant obstruction distal to the cystic duct. The classic cause is carcinoma of the head of the pancreas, which compresses the distal CBD so bile backs up and distends the gallbladder.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mirizzi syndrome is extrinsic compression of the common hepatic duct by a stone impacted in the cystic duct or Hartmann pouch; it presents with RUQ pain and cholecystitis features and a stone-filled, usually contracted gallbladder, not weight loss with a huge gallbladder and high CA19-9.
C. Distal CBD obstruction describes the level of the block, not its cause; the question asks for the cause, and weight loss with CA19-9 identifies it as pancreatic head cancer. A distal CBD stone would also give painful, fluctuating jaundice with a non-palpable gallbladder.
key_concept:
Courvoisier law: jaundice + palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be stones; think malignancy.
  • Pancreatic head/periampullary: distended gallbladder, dilated intra and extrahepatic ducts
  • Klatskin: shrunken gallbladder, intrahepatic dilation only
  • Stones: fibrosed non-palpable gallbladder, painful fluctuating jaundice
  • Clues to malignancy: weight loss, anorexia, high CA19-9
exam_pearl: 'Distal CBD obstruction' is a level, not a cause; when CA19-9 and weight loss are given, name the tumor.

stem: 68-year-old Male patient was complaining of yellowish discoloration, epigastric pain, dark urine, pale stool and weight loss. On examination the patient was jaundiced and on palpation tenderness in the epigastric region and right upper quadrant. The gallbladder was palpable and tender. Labs showed: Elevated liver enzymes, high total and direct bilirubin, high ALP, GGT 213, CA19-9: 502. Ultrasound showed hugely dilated common bile duct and gallbladder. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
OptD: Cancer of the head of the pancreas
highlight_terms_source: dark urine, pale stool and weight loss
hugely dilated common bile duct and gallbladder
why_right: A 68-year-old with weight loss, obstructive jaundice (dark urine, pale stool, high direct bilirubin, ALP, GGT), a palpable gallbladder, hugely dilated CBD and gallbladder on ultrasound and CA19-9 502 has malignant distal biliary obstruction. The most likely cause is cancer of the head of the pancreas, which blocks the distal CBD and distends the gallbladder (Courvoisier sign).
why_wrong_block:
A. Mirizzi syndrome obstructs the common hepatic duct from a stone in the cystic duct/Hartmann pouch, so the CBD below it is not dilated and the gallbladder is usually stone-filled and contracted; it does not explain weight loss or CA19-9 of 502.
B. Liver metastases cause hepatomegaly and intrahepatic or hilar obstruction at most; they do not produce a hugely dilated CBD with a distended gallbladder.
C. Distal CBD obstruction is the anatomical level shown on ultrasound, not the underlying cause; the question asks for the cause, and age, weight loss and CA19-9 point to a pancreatic head tumor.
key_concept:
Where the duct dilation stops tells you where the block is.
  • Dilated CBD + distended gallbladder: distal block (pancreatic head, ampulla, distal CBD)
  • Intrahepatic dilation only + collapsed gallbladder: hilar Klatskin tumor
  • Dilated CHD with normal CBD + cystic duct stone: Mirizzi
  • Malignancy clues: age, weight loss, high CA19-9
  • Next imaging: contrast CT (double duct sign)
exam_pearl: Courvoisier classically describes a non-tender gallbladder; a tender one here does not overturn the weight loss, huge CBD and CA19-9.

stem: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the Paediatric Outpatient Clinic because she is already showing breast development, appearance of pubic hair and acne. She is otherwise asymptomatic. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: breast development, appearance of pubic hair and acne
why_right: A 7 year old girl with breast development, then pubic hair and acne, who is "otherwise asymptomatic", is showing pubertal signs in their normal order. A normal sequence means the whole hypothalamic pituitary gonadal axis has switched on early, which is central (gonadotropin dependent) precocious puberty. In girls this is idiopathic in the large majority, so it is the most likely diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ovarian tumour: a peripheral (gonadotropin independent) source with suppressed LH and FSH and an out of order sequence; suspect it with rapid isolated estrogen effects, a pelvic mass or early vaginal bleeding.
C. Gonadotropin releasing tumour: rare and usually comes with other features; idiopathic central disease is far more likely in a well girl.
D. CNS lesion: an identifiable cause of central precocious puberty, but much more often found in boys or with neurological signs (headache, visual change); this girl is asymptomatic.
key_concept:
Normal sequence of pubertal signs = central; abnormal sequence = peripheral.
  • Central: pubertal LH/FSH, gonads make the steroids, always isosexual
  • Peripheral: prepubertal LH/FSH, source can be gonad, adrenal, ectopic or exogenous; iso or contrasexual
  • Girls: central is mostly idiopathic; boys: look harder for a CNS lesion
  • Workup: bone age, basal and GnRH stimulated LH, brain MRI
  • Treatment of central: GnRH agonist
exam_pearl: A boy with the same picture, or any girl with neurological signs, pushes you toward a CNS lesion.

stem: In which of the following conditions would you expect a bone age greater than the chronologic age?
why_right: The question asks where bone age exceeds chronological age. In congenital adrenal hyperplasia excess adrenal androgens accelerate epiphyseal maturation, so bone age runs ahead. These children are tall early but fuse early, ending with short adult height.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hypothyroidism: thyroid hormone is needed for skeletal maturation, so bone age is markedly delayed.
B. Chronic renal failure: chronic illness slows growth and delays bone age.
C. Familial short stature: bone age equals chronological age; the child is simply following short parents.
key_concept:
Sex steroid excess advances bone age; most growth failure delays it.
  • Advanced: CAH, precocious puberty, obesity, exogenous sex steroids
  • Delayed: hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, chronic illness (CKD, IBD), constitutional delay
  • Normal: familial short stature
  • CAH: commonest cause 21 hydroxylase deficiency; raised 17 hydroxyprogesterone
exam_pearl: Tall child now but short adult = advanced bone age from androgens or estrogens.

stem: A child with tall stature, long arms and fingers, following up with ophthalmology due to eye problems. On examination, he has mental retardation and skin bruising. What is his diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: tall stature, long arms and fingers
why_right: Tall stature with long arms and fingers plus an eye problem fits both Marfan syndrome and homocystinuria (marfanoid habitus with lens dislocation). The discriminating clue is mental retardation: intellectual disability is a feature of homocystinuria, while intelligence is normal in Marfan. Homocystinuria also carries a thrombotic tendency and osteoporosis, which Marfan does not.
why_wrong_block: A. Marfan: shares the tall habitus, arachnodactyly and ectopia lentis, but intelligence is normal; choose it when the picture adds aortic root dilation, mitral valve prolapse or pectus deformity with a normal intellect.
key_concept:
Marfan vs homocystinuria: same habitus, separated by intellect, lens direction and clotting.
  • Marfan: autosomal dominant, fibrillin 1; lens dislocates upward; aortic root dilation; normal IQ
  • Homocystinuria: autosomal recessive, cystathionine beta synthase deficiency; lens dislocates downward
  • Homocystinuria: intellectual disability, thromboembolism, osteoporosis
  • Other mimics: Ehlers Danlos (skin hyperelasticity, bruising), Klinefelter (tall, small testes)
exam_pearl: Marfanoid child plus intellectual disability or thrombosis = homocystinuria, not Marfan.

stem: A child came for a routine check up. He can walk steadily independently, and has an immature pincer grasp. Says 4-6 words, knows 2 body parts. What is the developmental age in months?
why_right: Place the child at the oldest milestone he has achieved. "Walks steadily independently" is past the 12 month stage of first steps, and the language clues are the decisive ones: about 4 to 6 words and knowing 2 body parts both belong to 15 months. The "immature pincer grasp" is a 9 month skill he has already passed, so it does not limit the age. He is not yet at the 18 month vocabulary of 6 to 10 words, so 15 months fits best.
why_wrong_block:
A. 24 months: expect 2 word phrases, about 50 words, climbing stairs and a 6 block tower; none are described.
B. 18 months: expect running and a vocabulary of 6 to 10 words; 4 to 6 words falls short.
D. 12 months: a child just starting to walk with only 1 to 3 words besides mama and dada; knowing body parts is later.
key_concept:
Developmental age = at or above the oldest achieved milestone, below the youngest missing one.
  • 12 m: walks alone, mature pincer, 1 to 3 words besides mama/dada, imitates
  • 15 m: walks well and backward, 3 to 6 words, points to body parts, uses spoon, 2 cube tower
  • 18 m: runs, 6 to 10 words, 4 cube tower, pours pellets from bottle
  • 24 m: 2 word phrases, about 50 words, stairs, 6 cube tower
exam_pearl: Word count is the tiebreaker: 4 to 6 words with body parts = 15 months; 6 to 10 words = 18 months.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Repeated below as 'Q:' version with Answer: C.

stem: Babay walking steady gate with wide steps and (rising both arms while walking) > i think the arm was like this im sure from the meaning
why_right: A wide based gait with both arms raised (the high guard posture) is the gait of a new independent walker, who keeps a broad base and lifts the arms for balance. Independent walking normally begins around 12 months and is established by about 15 months, so among these options 14 months is the age that fits a child who is walking alone but still with the immature high guard pattern.
why_wrong_block:
A. 8 m: at this age the child is sitting and starting to crawl; independent walking is not expected.
B. 9 m: pulls to stand and cruises at most; walking alone with any gait pattern is too early.
D. 15 m: by now walking is usually mature enough to walk backward, with arms lowered and a narrower base; the raised arm posture points slightly younger.
key_concept:
Early independent gait: wide base, arms high (high guard), short steps.
  • 9 m: pulls to stand, cruising
  • 12 m: first independent steps, wide base, arms raised
  • 15 m: walks well, walks backward, arms come down
  • 18 m: runs
exam_pearl: Arms up for balance = brand new walker (about 12 to 14 months); walking backward = 15 months.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Related variant recall under 1904.

stem: A baby is observed walking independently with a wide-based gait and arms raised for balance. At approximately what age is a child typically expected to walk independently with a wide-based gait and arms raised for balance?
highlight_terms_source: walking independently with a wide-based gait and arms raised for balance
why_right: The lead in asks when a child is typically expected to walk independently with a wide based gait and arms raised for balance. That high guard posture marks the onset of independent walking, which is a 12 month milestone. The broad base and raised arms are compensations for immature balance in the first weeks of walking.
why_wrong_block:
A. 9 months: the child pulls to stand and may cruise along furniture, but does not walk alone.
C. 15 months: walking is more mature by now (walks well, walks backward) and the arms are usually lowered.
key_concept:
Walking ladder:
  • 9 m: pulls to stand, cruises
  • 12 m: walks alone with wide base and arms raised
  • 15 m: walks well and backward
  • 18 m: runs
  • 24 m: up and down stairs
exam_pearl: Asked for the typical age, not a range: independent walking with high guard = 12 months.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Related variant recall under 1904.

stem: Child walking unsteady with raising hands when walking. How old is he in months:
why_right: "Walking unsteady with raising hands" describes the beginner walker: arms up in high guard to balance and an unstable, wide based gait. This is the picture of a child who has just started walking independently, the 12 month milestone.
why_wrong_block:
A. 15: walking is steadier by now, the child can walk backward and the arms have come down.
B. 18: the child runs and kicks a ball; an unsteady arms up gait would be immature for this age.
D. 24: the child climbs stairs and throws overhand; an unsteady beginner gait at 2 years would be delayed.
key_concept:
Gait matures fast after the first steps:
  • 12 m: unsteady, wide base, arms raised
  • 15 m: walks well, backward
  • 18 m: runs, kicks ball
  • 24 m: stairs, throws overhand
exam_pearl: Unsteady with hands up = 12 months; still like this at 18 months or later should prompt assessment.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Related variant recall under 1904.

stem: Baby with immature pincer grip, can say 5 to 6 words, and pointed 2 parts of his body, age in months
why_right: The decisive clues are language: 5 to 6 words and pointing to 2 body parts. Pointing to body parts is a 15 month skill and 3 to 6 words belongs to 15 months, while a vocabulary of 6 to 10 words is reached at 18 months. A child sitting at the top of the 15 month range but not yet at 18 months fits 17 months best among these options.
why_wrong_block:
A. 12: only 1 to 3 words besides mama and dada are expected and body part identification is not yet present.
C. 19: by now the child would be past the 18 month level with 6 to 10 words; 5 to 6 words is still below it.
D. 24: expect about 50 words and 2 word phrases; this child is well short of that.
key_concept:
Vocabulary ladder (single words):
  • 12 m: 1 to 3 words besides mama/dada
  • 15 m: 3 to 6 words, points to body parts
  • 18 m: 6 to 10 words
  • 24 m: about 50 words, 2 word phrases
  • 36 m: about 100 words, 3 word sentences
exam_pearl: Same options, different key: 5 to 6 words = 17 months (below 18); 6 to 10 words = 19 months (at or above 18).

stem: child can walk alone, steadily. Immature pincer grasp. Say 6-10 words and points to 2 body parts, how old is he by month?
why_right: The oldest milestone achieved is the vocabulary: 6 to 10 words is the 18 month level, so the child is at least 18 months. Steady independent walking and pointing to 2 body parts are earlier skills he has passed, and there are no 2 year skills such as 2 word phrases. The option at or just above 18 months and below 24 months is 19.
why_wrong_block:
A. 12: a child at 12 months is just starting to walk and has only 1 to 3 words besides mama and dada.
B. 17: fits 3 to 6 words with body parts; a full 6 to 10 word vocabulary means the 18 month level is reached.
D. 24: expect about 50 words and 2 word phrases, which are not described.
key_concept:
Age = at or above the oldest achieved milestone, below the youngest missing one.
  • 15 m: 3 to 6 words, points to body parts
  • 18 m: 6 to 10 words, runs
  • 24 m: about 50 words, 2 word phrases
exam_pearl: 6 to 10 words = 18 month level, so pick the option just above 18 (19), not the one below (17).

stem: Paedia walk back ward and use to eat spoon and from Age in month
why_right: The two clues are walking backward and using a spoon. Walking backward is a 15 month gross motor milestone, and starting to feed with a spoon (sloppily) is a 15 month self care skill. Both together place the child at 15 months.
why_wrong_block:
A. 12 month: the child has only just started walking forward and drinks from a cup; walking backward and spoon use come later.
C. 24 month: expect stairs, throwing overhand and 2 word phrases; a 2 year old would be described with those, not with first spoon use.
D. 9 month: pulls to stand and has an early pincer grasp; not walking at all.
key_concept:
15 month cluster:
  • Gross motor: walks well and backward
  • Fine motor: scribbles, 2 cube tower, inserts pellets into bottle
  • Self care: uses spoon (messily), helps in housework
  • Language: 3 to 6 words, follows commands, points to body parts
  • Uses spoon well, spilling little = 3 years
exam_pearl: Spoon used sloppily = 15 months; spoon used well = 3 years.

stem: A child brought by his mother to well baby clinic. On history and examination Language: say 2-3 words other than Mama & Dada Fine motor: walks backwards Cognitive: Stacks 2 blocks Social: follow one step command How old is the child?
highlight_terms_source: say 2-3 words other than Mama & Dada
why_right: Label each finding with its milestone age: walks backwards, stacks 2 blocks and follows a one step command are all 15 month skills. Saying 2 to 3 words besides mama and dada is a 12 month skill that is already achieved. The oldest milestones achieved sit at 15 months, so the child is 15 months.
why_wrong_block:
A. At 9 months the child only pulls to stand and says mama/dada nonspecifically; walking backwards and following commands are far beyond 9 months.
B. 12 months explains the extra words, but walking backwards, a 2 block tower and following one step commands are 15 month skills, so the child is older than 12 months.
D. A 24 month old walks up and down stairs, stacks about 6 blocks and puts 2 words together; this child shows none of these, so 24 months is too old.
key_concept:
Developmental age = the oldest milestone achieved, below the youngest one not achieved.
  • 12 months: walks, 2 to 3 words besides mama/dada, block in cup
  • 15 months: walks backward, tower of 2, 3 to 6 words, follows simple commands, uses spoon sloppily
  • 18 months: runs, tower of 4, 6 to 10 words
  • 24 months: stairs, tower of 6, 2 word phrases
exam_pearl: Walking backwards and a 2 block tower are the 15 month signature; do not stop at 12 months because of the word count.

stem: A child is assessed for developmental milestones. Findings include: Gross motor: walks backwards Fine motor: eats with spoon Language: speaks 5-6 words Social: plays with cubes What is the age in months?
why_right: Walks backwards is a 15 month gross motor skill, eats with a spoon (sloppily) appears at 15 months, and 5 to 6 words fits the 15 month range of 3 to 6 words. Playing with cubes is consistent with stacking 2 blocks at this age. All findings cluster at 15 months.
why_wrong_block:
A. A 6 month old sits alone, transfers objects and babbles; walking and real words are impossible at 6 months.
B. At 9 months the child pulls to stand and says mama/dada nonspecifically; walking backwards, spoon use and 5 to 6 words are well beyond 9 months.
D. At 24 months the child climbs stairs, uses about 50 words and joins 2 words into phrases; 5 to 6 single words is too few for 24 months.
key_concept:
Match each domain to its age, then pick the age where most findings converge.
  • 15 months: walks backward, uses spoon (sloppily), 3 to 6 words, tower of 2, follows simple commands
  • 18 months: runs, 6 to 10 words, tower of 4
  • 24 months: about 50 words, 2 word phrases, stairs
exam_pearl: Word count helps: 2 to 3 words at 12 months, up to 6 at 15 months, 6 to 10 at 18 months, about 50 at 24 months.

stem: Child came for routine check up. He can transfer objects hand-to-hand but hasn't developed pincer grasp. What is the developmental age in months?
key_concept:
Lower limit = oldest skill achieved; upper limit = youngest skill not achieved.
  • Transfer hand to hand, palmar grasp, sits alone: 6 months
  • Immature pincer grasp: 9 months
  • Mature pincer grasp: 12 months
  • Transfer present + no pincer = 6 to 8 months
exam_pearl: If the expected answer (about 7 months) is missing, the recall is probably garbled; learn the bracket, not the option.

stem: While at the clinic, an infant craw toward the doctor, rolls over, sits briefly, transfers objects from hand to hand and grasps objects using his radial palm. The infant is unable to use a pincer grasp. What is the approximate age in months?
highlight_terms_source: transfers objects from hand to hand
unable to use a pincer grasp
why_right: Transfers objects hand to hand and radial palmar grasp are 6 month skills, rolling over and sitting briefly fit 6 months, and crawling appears at 6 to 9 months. The infant is unable to use a pincer grasp, which appears at 9 months, so the age is above 6 but below 9 months: 7 months.
why_wrong_block:
A. At 3 months the infant only holds the head up and follows objects; crawling, sitting and transferring are not possible yet.
B. At 5 months the infant reaches and rolls front to back, but hand to hand transfer, sitting and crawling are 6 month or later skills.
D. At 9 months a pincer grasp is present; its absence here means the infant is younger than 9 months.
key_concept:
The skill the child cannot yet do sets the upper limit of the age.
  • 4 months: reaches, rolls prone to supine, no head lag
  • 6 months: sits, transfers, palmar grasp, rolls both ways
  • 6 to 9 months: crawls
  • 9 months: pincer grasp, pulls to stand
exam_pearl: Transfer present but no pincer grasp = between 6 and 9 months; pick the option inside that window.

stem: An infant lies with his head to one side and raises his head slightly, but the head lags when pulling up to a sitting position. The infant smiles when involved in social interactions and follows moving objects 180 degrees, but does not attempt to reach for them. What is the approximate developmental age in weeks?
why_right: Social smile and following objects 180 degrees are 2 month milestones. Head lag disappears and reaching begins at 4 months, so head lag on pull to sit and no attempt to reach place the infant below 4 months. 2 months in the unit asked is 8 weeks.
why_wrong_block:
A. At 4 weeks (1 month) social smiling and tracking through 180 degrees are not yet expected.
C. By 12 weeks (3 months) a prone infant lifts the head about 45 degrees with steadier control; here the head is raised only slightly, and every finding is already explained by the 8 week (2 month) milestones.
D. At 16 weeks (4 months) head lag has gone and the infant reaches for objects, both absent here.
key_concept:
Early infant milestones (convert to weeks when asked):
  • 2 months (8 weeks): social smile, coos, tracks past midline / 180 degrees
  • 4 months (16 weeks): no head lag, reaches, laughs, rolls front to back
exam_pearl: Read the unit: the question asks for weeks, so 2 months becomes 8 weeks.

stem: A newborn who is following objects 180 degrees, no head lag when pulled to sitting position, social smiling. Age by weeks?
why_right: Social smile and 180 degree tracking are 2 month skills, but the decisive clue is no head lag when pulled to sitting, which is achieved at 4 months. 4 months in weeks is 16 weeks, so the infant is at least 16 weeks developmentally (the word 'newborn' in the stem is loose wording).
why_wrong_block:
A. Read as 4 weeks (1 month), a social smile and 180 degree tracking are not yet expected, and head lag is still marked; 4 years is plainly far too old.
B. 8 weeks (2 months) fits the social smile and tracking, but head lag is still present at 2 months; here it has resolved.
C. At 12 weeks head control is improving, but full disappearance of head lag on pull to sit is the 4 month (16 week) marker.
key_concept:
Head lag is the switch between 8 and 16 weeks.
  • Smile + 180 degree tracking + head lag present = 8 weeks
  • Smile + tracking + no head lag (and reaching) = 16 weeks
exam_pearl: Same stem pattern as the 8 week card; the presence or absence of head lag flips the answer.

stem: Pediatric patient presented in ER with fever and barky cough a long senario but he was in distress Bp was 80/60, Oxygen was 80% What is the appropriate initial management?
OptC: Some type of intubation in the OR
key_concept:
Barky cough + distress: grade severity, then treat the airway.
  • Mild croup (no stridor at rest): single dose dexamethasone
  • Moderate/severe (stridor at rest, retractions): nebulized epinephrine + steroid + oxygen
  • Impending failure (hypoxia, fatigue, altered consciousness): secure airway
  • Toxic, high fever, drooling, tripod: epiglottitis, prepare for intubation + 3rd generation cephalosporin
  • Toxic with barky cough not responding to epinephrine: bacterial tracheitis
exam_pearl: SpO2 80% is never plain mild croup: oxygen and airway assessment come first, then look for severe croup versus a bacterial airway infection.

stem: A mother brings her 6-month-old baby with complaints of pancytopenia and organomegaly. Labs has low Hemoglobin What is the most likely type of leukemia?
why_right: A child with pancytopenia, organomegaly and low hemoglobin has bone marrow replacement with extramedullary infiltration, typical of acute leukemia. ALL is the most common childhood leukemia (and the most common childhood cancer), so it is the most likely type.
why_wrong_block:
A. AML is the second most common childhood leukemia; favour it when the stem gives myeloid clues such as Auer rods, gum infiltration or DIC.
B. CML is rare in children and presents with marked leukocytosis and splenomegaly in the chronic phase, not pancytopenia.
D. Acute non-lymphoblastic leukemia is another name for AML, which is less common than ALL in children.
key_concept:
Child + pancytopenia + hepatosplenomegaly/lymphadenopathy = think acute leukemia; ALL is the most common.
  • ALL: most common childhood leukemia, peak in early childhood
  • AML (= acute non-lymphoblastic): second most common
  • CML: rare in children
exam_pearl: 'Acute non-lymphoblastic' is just AML in old wording; do not treat it as a separate answer.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1674).

stem: When do Screening for paedia for Irion defiency anemia?
why_right: Universal screening for anemia (hemoglobin/CBC) is done at 9 to 12 months, so 12 months is the screening age. Iron stores from birth are used up around 6 to 9 months while dietary iron is often low, which is why the screen is timed near the first birthday.
why_wrong_block:
A. 6 months is too early for routine screening in a healthy term infant; earlier testing is only for risk factors such as prematurity or low birth weight.
C. 15 to 18 months is the repeat screen for children with an underlying condition causing anemia, not the initial universal screen.
D. 24 months is too late for the initial screen; iron deficiency could already have affected development.
key_concept:
Well baby screening timing:
  • Anemia (CBC/Hb): all children at 9 to 12 months
  • Repeat at 15 to 18 months if an underlying anemia causing condition
  • Autism screening: around 2 years
exam_pearl: 18 months is the repeat (risk) screen, not the first one.

stem: Paedia with febrile convulsion her mother give paracetamol every 4h for 3days cae c/o jundice whate is case
key_concept:
Paracetamol toxicity stages:
  • Stage 1 (first 24 h): nausea, vomiting, malaise, normal labs
  • Stage 2 (days 2 to 3): RUQ pain, rising transaminases
  • Stage 3 (days 3 to 4): jaundice, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, liver failure
  • Repeated or unknown timing ingestion: no nomogram; send level + LFTs and start N-acetylcysteine
exam_pearl: Count the doses: every 4 hours around the clock is 6 doses a day, and jaundice from paracetamol liver injury typically appears around day 3.

stem: Paedia ingestion of 20 tablets of iron how to do
why_right: The terse stem gives only "20 tablets of iron" in a child, which is a large, potentially toxic ingestion (the matching full question adds GI bleeding and tachycardia a few hours later). Symptomatic or severe iron poisoning is treated with chelation, and the specific antidote is parenteral (IV) deferoxamine, which binds free iron so it can be excreted in urine.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observation: acceptable only for a small, clearly non-toxic ingestion in a child who stays well with a normal serum iron; a large ingestion in a sick child needs active treatment, and the quiet latent phase can falsely reassure.
B. Gastric lavage: removes iron tablets poorly and does not treat the absorbed iron; it is not the definitive treatment once the child is symptomatic. Chelation is.
key_concept:
Iron overdose: symptomatic or high serum iron = IV deferoxamine.
  • Stage I (first hours): vomiting, abdominal pain, haematemesis, diarrhoea
  • Stage II: latent phase, falsely reassuring
  • Stage III: shock, metabolic acidosis, CNS depression
  • Stage IV: hepatotoxicity
  • Stage V: GI strictures/obstruction weeks later
  • Activated charcoal does NOT bind iron
exam_pearl: Antidote pairs: iron = deferoxamine; paracetamol = N-acetylcysteine. Do not be fooled by the latent phase.

stem: A 5-year-old child presents with drowsiness, abdominal pain, nausea and bloody diarrhea after ingesting an unknown number of iron tablets several hours before (see lab result). Test Result Normal Value: Iron 94 (9-21.5 umol/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
highlight_terms_source: ingesting an unknown number of iron tablets
why_right: The child is clearly poisoned: "drowsiness" (CNS depression) plus "bloody diarrhea" after iron tablets, and a serum iron of 94 umol/L, several times the upper normal limit of 21.5. Symptomatic iron toxicity with a markedly raised level is the indication for chelation with IV deferoxamine.
why_wrong_block:
A. Haemodialysis: does not effectively remove iron itself; it is used to clear the iron deferoxamine complex if renal failure develops.
B. Gastric lavage: poor at removing iron tablets and not useful several hours later in a symptomatic child; it does not treat absorbed iron.
C. Oral activated charcoal: does not bind iron (nor lithium, alcohols or other metals), so it is ineffective here. Right for many other recent toxic ingestions.
key_concept:
Iron poisoning: treat the sick child with chelation.
  • Indications for IV deferoxamine: GI bleeding, shock, metabolic acidosis, altered consciousness, or very high serum iron
  • Charcoal: does not bind iron
  • Dialysis: only for the chelate in renal failure
exam_pearl: Drowsiness plus bloody diarrhoea after iron tablets = severe toxicity; go straight to IV deferoxamine.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Question is a screenshot on the next page; option D marked with ** in the screenshot.

stem: 7-year-old child have neck stiffness and all meningitis symptoms. His CSF was obtained, and Gram stain showed Grampositive cocci Which chemoprophylaxis should be offered to his contacts?
key_concept:
Match the Gram stain to the bug, then the prophylaxis.
  • Gram-positive diplococci = pneumococcus: no contact prophylaxis
  • Gram-negative diplococci = meningococcus: rifampicin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone
  • Gram-negative coccobacilli = Hib: rifampicin
  • Child contact: rifampicin; pregnant contact: ceftriaxone
  • A version of this stem with Gram-negative coccobacilli (Hib) is answered with rifampicin
  • Patient himself: ceftriaxone + vancomycin (+ dexamethasone)
exam_pearl: Prophylaxis is about the organism, not the word "meningitis": pneumococcus spreads poorly and contacts need nothing.

stem: A pediatric patient has been diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. His brother and sister, who live in the same household, are asymptomatic. Which of the following regimens is appropriate for chemoprophylaxis in these close contacts?
why_right: Household contacts of meningococcal disease need chemoprophylaxis whether or not they have symptoms. Of the regimens listed, a single dose of ciprofloxacin is the only correct, standard regimen and it is the agent best suited to Neisseria meningitidis. The other options use the wrong drug or the wrong number of doses.
why_wrong_block:
A. Penicillin and rifampin for 1 week: penicillin does not clear nasopharyngeal carriage, and rifampicin prophylaxis is a short 2-day course, not a week. Right when only rifampicin for 2 days is offered for a child contact.
C. Penicillin for 1 week: penicillin treats invasive disease but does not eradicate carriage, so it is not used for prophylaxis. It is not right for any contact prophylaxis scenario.
D. IM ceftriaxone 4 doses: ceftriaxone is a valid prophylactic agent (preferred in pregnancy) but as a single IM dose; multiple doses is a treatment-type regimen, not prophylaxis.
key_concept:
Meningococcal contact prophylaxis: give to close/household contacts, symptomatic or not, as soon as possible.
  • Ciprofloxacin: single oral dose, best for N. meningitidis
  • Rifampicin: 2-day course; classic choice for children and for Hib contacts
  • Ceftriaxone: single IM dose; choice in pregnancy
  • Penicillin does not clear carriage, so it is never prophylaxis
  • Hajj pilgrims need meningococcal vaccination
exam_pearl: The count matters: ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone are single doses, rifampicin is 2 days; any option giving a week or multiple ceftriaxone doses is wrong.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1755).

stem: 2 year old pt want to go for hajj he didn't take any Prevention meningococcal vaccine what the best method of prophylaxis antibiotic
why_right: The question asks for antibiotic prophylaxis against meningococcus for a "2 year old" travelling to Hajj without the vaccine. In a young child the classic oral agent is rifampicin twice daily for 2 days; ciprofloxacin is given as a single dose, mainly to adults, and ceftriaxone as a single IM dose.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cefdinir 5 days BID: an oral cephalosporin for otitis, sinusitis or pharyngitis; it does not reliably eradicate nasopharyngeal meningococcal carriage and is not a prophylaxis regimen.
C. Ciprofloxacin 3 days BID: ciprofloxacin prophylaxis is a single oral dose, not a 3 day course, and exam keys favour rifampicin for a young child.
D. Ceftriaxone 5 days OD: ceftriaxone prophylaxis is a single IM dose (useful in pregnancy); a 5 day course is a treatment regimen, not prophylaxis.
key_concept:
Meningococcal chemoprophylaxis regimens.
  • Rifampicin: oral, twice daily for 2 days (children)
  • Hib contacts: rifampicin once daily for 4 days
  • Ciprofloxacin: single oral dose, adults
  • Ceftriaxone: single IM dose, pregnancy
  • Meningococcal ACYW135 vaccine is mandatory before Hajj
  • Pilgrims from the African meningitis belt: vaccine plus chemoprophylaxis on arrival
exam_pearl: Prophylaxis is short: rifampicin 2 days or a single dose of cipro/ceftriaxone; any 3 to 5 day course is a distractor.

stem: A newborn infant born from a mother with polyhydramnios presents with excessive salivation along with coughing and choking with the first oral feeding. An x-rav of the abdomen shows gas in stomach and a nasogastric tube coiled in the esophagus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: coughing and choking with the first oral feeding
nasogastric tube coiled in the esophagus
why_right: Maternal "polyhydramnios" (the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid), "excessive salivation", and "coughing and choking with the first oral feeding" mean the oesophagus ends blindly, confirmed by the "nasogastric tube coiled in the esophagus". The decisive clue is "gas in stomach": air can only reach the stomach through a distal fistula between trachea and lower oesophagus, so this is oesophageal atresia with distal TEF, the commonest type.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oesophageal atresia alone: would also coil the NG tube, but with no fistula the abdomen is gasless; gas in the stomach rules it out.
B. Tracheoesophageal fistula alone (H-type): the oesophagus is patent so the NG tube passes into the stomach; it presents later with recurrent chest infections and choking with feeds.
D. Omphalocele: a midline abdominal wall defect with bowel covered by a membrane at the umbilicus, visible at birth; it does not stop an NG tube.
E. Gastroschisis: uncovered bowel herniating to the right of the umbilicus; an abdominal wall defect, not an oesophageal one.
key_concept:
Coiled NG tube = oesophageal atresia; then look at the abdomen.
  • Gas in stomach = EA with distal TEF (commonest)
  • Gasless abdomen = isolated EA (or proximal fistula only)
  • NG passes, recurrent pneumonia = H-type TEF
  • Polyhydramnios + drooling + choking on first feed
  • Screen for VACTERL anomalies
exam_pearl: Gas in the stomach is the clue that upgrades "oesophageal atresia" to "atresia with TEF".

stem: Newborn has bubbling mucus and fluid from the nose after the first feed, xray revealed NGT coiled in esophageal pouch, which of the following is the diagnosis ?
highlight_terms_source: bubbling mucus and fluid from the nose after the first feed
why_right: "Bubbling mucus and fluid" after the "first feed" with an "NGT coiled in esophageal pouch" is the oesophageal atresia/tracheoesophageal fistula complex. Oesophageal atresia is not offered, and the commonest form of this anomaly is atresia with a distal fistula, so tracheoesophageal fistula is the keyed answer for this anomaly among the choices.
why_wrong_block:
B. Choanal atresia: causes cyanosis at rest that improves with crying and a catheter cannot pass through the nose; the oesophagus is normal, so an NG tube passed by mouth would not coil.
C. Tracheomalacia: a floppy trachea causes expiratory stridor and noisy breathing that worsens with crying or feeds; it does not block an NG tube.
key_concept:
Coiled NG tube = EA/TEF complex.
  • Most common type: proximal blind pouch + distal TEF (gas in stomach)
  • Clues: polyhydramnios, drooling, frothy secretions, choking on first feed
  • Choanal atresia: cyanosis relieved by crying
  • Tracheomalacia: stridor, tube passes
exam_pearl: If "oesophageal atresia" is missing from the options, pick TEF: they come together in most cases.

stem: A newborn presents with excessive drooling, bubbling from the mouth, and an inability to pass a nasogastric (NG) tube. Xray reveals the NG tube coiled in the upper esophageal pouch. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: inability to pass a nasogastric (NG) tube
NG tube coiled in the upper esophageal pouch
why_right: "Excessive drooling", "bubbling from the mouth" and an "inability to pass a nasogastric tube" that is seen "coiled in the upper esophageal pouch" are the defining picture of a blind-ending oesophagus, which is oesophageal atresia. The stem gives no abdominal gas finding, so the atresia itself is the diagnosis being asked.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hiatus hernia: stomach herniating through the diaphragm causes reflux and vomiting, but the NG tube still passes into the stomach.
C. Tracheoesophageal fistula: an isolated (H-type) fistula leaves the oesophagus patent so the tube passes; it presents with choking and recurrent chest infections. A fistula would be added only if gas is seen in the stomach.
D. Choanal atresia: blocked posterior nasal passages cause cyanosis that improves with crying and failure to pass a catheter through the nose into the pharynx, not a tube coiled in the oesophagus.
key_concept:
Coiled NG tube in an upper pouch = oesophageal atresia.
  • Clinical: drooling, frothy secretions, choking/cyanosis with feeds, maternal polyhydramnios
  • Gas in stomach: add distal TEF
  • Tube passes + recurrent pneumonia: H-type TEF
  • Cyanosis relieved by crying: choanal atresia
exam_pearl: The NG tube is the test: stuck in the chest = atresia; passes but chokes on feeds = H-type fistula.
