stem: Child Had URTI 2 Days Ago, Presented With Erythematous Rash That Covers The Jaw And Extends To The Shoulder And Back, WITHOUT Desquamation And Occipital, Posterior Cervical, Post Auricular Lymphadenopathy (Written In Case Like This):
highlight_terms_source: Occipital, Posterior Cervical, Post Auricular Lymphadenopathy
why_right: A mild prodrome ("URTI 2 days ago") followed by a pink-red rash that starts high on the face/jaw and spreads down to the "shoulder and back", plus "occipital, posterior cervical, post auricular lymphadenopathy", is classic rubella. Suboccipital and postauricular nodes are the hallmark that separates it from the other exanthems.
why_wrong_block:
B. Adenovirus: causes pharyngoconjunctival fever (fever, sore throat, conjunctivitis); a rash is non-specific and the occipital/postauricular node pattern is not typical.
C. Measles: high fever with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots before a rash that starts behind the ears/hairline; it is a much sicker child and nodes are generalized rather than postauricular-predominant.
D. Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19): "slapped cheek" facial redness then a lacy reticular rash on the limbs, with no prominent lymphadenopathy.
key_concept:
Viral exanthem forks.
  • Rubella: mild, low-grade fever, postauricular/suboccipital nodes, face-to-trunk pink rash, Forchheimer spots
  • Measles: high fever, 3Cs, Koplik spots
  • Parvovirus B19: slapped cheek, lacy limb rash
  • Roseola: high fever, rash appears as fever breaks
  • Scarlet fever: sandpaper rash then desquamation
exam_pearl: Postauricular plus suboccipital lymph nodes = rubella until proven otherwise.

stem: A 6-year-old unvaccinated girl is brought to the clinic by her mother with low-grade fever, rash, and swollen glands. Her mother reports The child was well until 2 days ago. Then developed mild fever, runny nose, and red eyes Yesterday, she developed a pink, non-itchy rash that started on the face and then spread to thetrunk and limbs What the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: pink, non-itchy rash that started on the face
why_right: An unvaccinated child with a "low-grade fever", mild coryza and red eyes, "swollen glands", and a "pink, non-itchy rash" that "started on the face" and spread to the trunk and limbs fits rubella. The mild course, low-grade fever and lymphadenopathy, with no Koplik spots, separate it from measles.
why_wrong_block:
A. Measles: shares the face-to-body spread and coryza/conjunctivitis, but presents with a HIGH fever, a sick child and Koplik spots before a darker, confluent rash; none of that is described here.
C. Epstein-Barr virus: infectious mononucleosis gives exudative pharyngitis, fatigue, generalized nodes and splenomegaly; a rash mainly appears after amoxicillin, not as a face-to-trunk pink exanthem.
key_concept:
Measles vs rubella hinges on severity.
  • Rubella: low-grade fever, mild, pink discrete rash, postauricular/suboccipital nodes
  • Measles: high fever, 3Cs, Koplik spots, ill child
  • EBV: sore throat, splenomegaly, rash after amoxicillin
exam_pearl: Same stem with HIGH fever and white oral spots flips the answer to measles.

stem: A 6-year-old child presents with a high-grade fever, malaise, conjunctivitis, coryza, and a cough. A rash of discrete pink macules recently began on the face and extends to the hands and feet. The child also had small, whitish spots inside the mouth before the rash appeared. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: small, whitish spots inside the mouth before the rash appeared
why_right: A "high-grade fever" with the 3Cs ("conjunctivitis, coryza, and a cough") and "small, whitish spots inside the mouth before the rash appeared" (Koplik spots, pathognomonic) followed by a rash starting on the face and spreading to the hands and feet is measles.
why_wrong_block:
A. Toxic shock syndrome: high fever with hypotension and a diffuse sunburn-like erythroderma that later desquamates, often linked to tampons or wounds; no Koplik spots or 3Cs.
B. Gonococcal bacteremia: a few acral pustules with arthritis/tenosynovitis in a sexually active patient, not a viral prodrome with a face-to-limb rash.
D. Rubella: similar face-to-body rash but with only low-grade fever, a mild illness, postauricular nodes and no Koplik spots.
key_concept:
Measles = high fever + 3Cs + Koplik spots, then rash.
  • Rash starts at hairline/face and spreads downward
  • Koplik spots: white spots on buccal mucosa opposite molars, before the rash
  • Rubella: low-grade fever, no Koplik
  • Complications: pneumonia, encephalitis, SSPE
exam_pearl: High vs low fever plus Koplik spots is the single switch between measles and rubella on this stem.

stem: A 5-year-old childis brought to the clinic with a febrile illness with a cough and separate irregularly shaped (blotchy) rashes. He has not had any routine vaccinations. On physical examination, there is enlarged tender cervical lymph nodes. There are also erythematous maculopapular rashes behind the ear, face and neck and to a lesser extent on the trunk. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: behind the ear, face and neck
why_right: An unvaccinated child with fever and cough and a blotchy, irregular erythematous maculopapular rash that begins behind the ears, face and neck and then spreads to the trunk to a lesser extent is the classic cephalocaudal measles exanthem. Measles rash tends to become confluent (blotchy), unlike the discrete pink macules of rubella, and the cough fits the measles prodrome (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis). Cervical lymphadenopathy is common in measles.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chickenpox gives itchy vesicles in crops at different stages (macule, papule, vesicle, crust), centred on the trunk; this rash is maculopapular and blotchy, not vesicular.
C. Mumps causes fever with parotid (or submandibular) gland swelling and no rash; think of it when the swelling is in front of the ear, not a rash behind it.
D. Rubella also spreads face to body, but it is a mild illness with low-grade fever, discrete pink macules that fade quickly and posterior auricular/suboccipital nodes; a prominent cough with a confluent blotchy rash points to measles.
key_concept:
Face-to-body maculopapular rash: decide measles vs rubella by severity, cough and rash texture.
  • Measles: high fever, 3 Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), Koplik spots, rash starts behind ears/hairline, becomes confluent/blotchy
  • Rubella: mild, low-grade fever, discrete pink macules, postauricular/suboccipital nodes
  • Varicella: vesicles in crops, trunk-centred
  • Mumps: parotitis, no rash
  • Unvaccinated status raises measles probability
exam_pearl: Rash starting behind the ears that turns blotchy and confluent in a coughing, unvaccinated child = measles; discrete pink macules in a well child = rubella.

stem: pediatric, rash in face or neck then go down, forgot it was desquamating or squamating not sure, no mention of murmur in qs , dx?
highlight_terms_source: rash in face or neck then go down
key_concept:
Face-down rash: measles vs rubella; desquamation shifts thinking toward Kawasaki (or scarlet fever).
  • Measles: 3 Cs + Koplik, confluent rash, fine branny peeling as it fades
  • Rubella: mild, discrete pink macules, posterior nodes
  • Kawasaki: fever ≥5 days + mucocutaneous signs, fingertip peeling later
  • Fifth disease: slapped cheek then lacy limb rash
exam_pearl: Peeling of the fingertips after prolonged fever is Kawasaki; fine branny peeling of a fading cephalocaudal rash after a cough/coryza prodrome is measles.

stem: A child is brought to Paediatric Clinic with cough, fever, rhinorrhoea, malaise, with conjunctival erythema. There are small, grayish, irregular lesions surrounded by an erythematous base, on the buccal mucus membrane near the second molar teeth. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: small, grayish, irregular lesions surrounded by an erythematous base, on the buccal mucus membrane near the second molar teeth
why_right: Small grayish lesions on an erythematous base on the buccal mucosa near the second molars are Koplik spots, which are pathognomonic for measles. Together with the prodrome of cough, rhinorrhoea (coryza) and conjunctival erythema (the 3 Cs) and fever, the diagnosis is measles, often before the rash appears.
why_wrong_block:
B. Rubella is a milder illness with discrete pink macules and posterior auricular/suboccipital nodes; it does not produce Koplik spots (any palatal petechiae are on the soft palate).
C. Parainfluenza causes croup: barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor; it has no buccal mucosal spots.
D. RSV causes bronchiolitis in infants: coryza followed by wheeze, crackles and respiratory distress; no Koplik spots or conjunctivitis-rash picture.
key_concept:
Koplik spots = measles until proven otherwise.
  • Prodrome: fever + cough, coryza, conjunctivitis
  • Koplik: grayish-white spots on red base, buccal mucosa opposite molars, appear before the rash
  • Rash: behind ears/face, spreads down, becomes confluent
  • Parainfluenza = croup; RSV = bronchiolitis
exam_pearl: Spots on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars = Koplik (measles); spots on the soft palate are not Koplik.

stem: A 2-year-old child weighing 12 kg is admitted to the pediatric ward for observation due to vomiting and poor oral intake. The medical team decides to initiate maintenance IV fluids. What is the appropriate daily fluid requirement for this child?
why_right: Maintenance fluid uses the Holliday-Segar rule: 100 mL/kg/day for the first 10 kg and 50 mL/kg/day for the next 10 kg. For a 12 kg child: 10 × 100 = 1000 mL plus 2 × 50 = 100 mL, giving 1100 mL/day. The child is only for observation with poor intake, so maintenance alone is asked, with no deficit added.
why_wrong_block:
A. 1200 mL comes from applying 100 mL/kg to all 12 kg; the kilograms above 10 kg are counted at only 50 mL/kg.
C. 1500 mL would be maintenance for a 20 kg child (1000 + 500); it overestimates for 12 kg and would only fit if a deficit were being added.
D. 1000 mL is the maintenance for exactly 10 kg; it ignores the extra 2 kg (another 100 mL).
key_concept:
Holliday-Segar daily maintenance:
  • First 10 kg: 100 mL/kg/day
  • Next 10 kg (11 to 20 kg): 50 mL/kg/day
  • Each kg above 20: 20 mL/kg/day
  • 12 kg: 1000 + 100 = 1100 mL/day
  • Hourly (4-2-1): 40 + 4 = 44 mL/h
exam_pearl: Do not multiply total weight by 100; only the first 10 kg get 100 mL/kg.

stem: A 14-month-old girt is brought to the clinic with vomi7ng and diarhoea. The mother reports her child is less ac7ve. On examina7on, she has mild dehydra7on with an es7mated fluid deficit of 5% (see lab results). Weigh 10 Kg Test Result Normal Values Sodium 128 134-146 mmol/L Potassium 3.3 3.5-5.1 mmol/L Chloride 94 97-108 mmol/L Bicarbonate 12 21-28 mmol/L How much intravenous fluid (mi/day) should be given?
why_right: Daily IV fluid = maintenance + deficit. Maintenance for 10 kg = 10 × 100 = 1000 mL. Deficit for 5% dehydration = 5% of 10 kg = 0.5 kg = 500 mL (weight × % × 10). Total = 1000 + 500 = 1500 mL/day. The low sodium, potassium and bicarbonate guide the fluid type and electrolyte replacement, not the volume.
why_wrong_block:
A. 1000 mL is maintenance only; it ignores the 5% deficit the stem tells you to replace.
B. 1250 mL adds only half the deficit (250 mL); the full 500 mL deficit belongs in the 24-hour total.
D. 1750 mL corresponds to a larger deficit (about 7.5%); the stem fixes the deficit at 5%.
key_concept:
Dehydration fluid volume = maintenance + deficit.
  • Maintenance: 100 mL/kg first 10 kg, 50 mL/kg next 10 kg, 20 mL/kg beyond
  • Deficit (mL) = weight (kg) × % dehydration × 10
  • 10 kg, 5%: 1000 + 500 = 1500 mL/day
  • Electrolytes (Na, K, HCO3) choose the fluid, not the volume
exam_pearl: When the stem gives a % deficit, add it to maintenance; answering maintenance alone (1000) is the trap.

stem: newborn with Maple Syrup ,What to give. A neonate presents with vomiting, lethargy, and signs of central nervous system depression. The baby has had episodes of seizures, and alternates between hypotonia and hypertonia. Diagnosed with maple syrup disease What's the treatment ?
OptC: Treat with high-dose sodium benzoate and sodium phenylacetate
OptD: Stop protein intake temporarily and start BCAA-free formula with IV glucose
why_right: Maple syrup urine disease is a defect in breaking down the branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine); leucine accumulation causes the neonatal encephalopathy described (vomiting, lethargy, seizures, alternating hypotonia/hypertonia). Acute management is to stop protein temporarily, give IV glucose (calories to stop catabolism) and then a BCAA-free formula; long term the diet restricts leucine, isoleucine and valine.
why_wrong_block:
A. This option is garbled in the recall and is not a recognized MSUD therapy; if it refers to nitisinone (NTBC), that drug is used for tyrosinemia type 1, not MSUD.
B. A phenylalanine-restricted diet treats phenylketonuria; MSUD needs restriction of the branched-chain amino acids, not phenylalanine.
C. Sodium benzoate and sodium phenylacetate are ammonia scavengers for hyperammonemia in urea cycle disorders, not the core treatment of MSUD.
key_concept:
Match the inborn error to its dietary fix:
  • MSUD: restrict leucine, isoleucine, valine (BCAA-free formula); acutely stop protein + IV glucose
  • PKU: restrict phenylalanine
  • Urea cycle disorders: sodium benzoate/phenylacetate, stop protein
  • Tyrosinemia type 1: nitisinone (NTBC)
exam_pearl: Sweet (maple syrup) smelling urine in an encephalopathic neonate = MSUD = branched-chain amino acids, not phenylalanine.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed recall 'newborn with Maple Syrup, What to give' plus screenshot with options (BCAA highlighted in red in option D). Q: Maple syrup urine disease: Restrict leucine, isoleucine and valine.

stem: A 70-year-old man complains that he cannot remember things, sometimes forgetting names of friends, famous community figures, and telephone numbers. His wife fears he has Alzheimer's disease. Physical examination is unremarkable apart from tender knee joints (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: forgetting names of friends, famous community figures, and telephone numbers
why_right: He sometimes forgets names and telephone numbers, with no reported impairment of daily function, no other cognitive or behavioral symptoms and an unremarkable examination (tender knees are incidental). Occasional retrieval lapses with preserved function are normal age-associated (benign) forgetfulness, not dementia. The worry comes from the wife, not from functional decline.
why_wrong_block:
A. Alzheimer disease is right when progressive memory loss for recent events interferes with daily activities (getting lost, repeating questions, failing to manage finances); none of that is described.
B. Lewy body dementia is right with fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, parkinsonism or REM sleep behavior disorder; none is present here.
D. Hypertensive encephalopathy is an acute emergency with severe hypertension, headache, confusion, seizures or visual changes; it is not a chronic mild memory complaint with a normal exam.
key_concept:
Dementia needs cognitive decline that impairs daily function.
  • Benign forgetfulness: occasional lapses, later recalled, function intact
  • Alzheimer: insidious recent memory loss, functional decline
  • Lewy body: fluctuations, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism
  • Vascular: stepwise or executive dysfunction, vascular risk factors
  • NPH: gait disturbance, incontinence, confusion
exam_pearl: The patient complaining about his own memory (rather than family noticing decline) with intact function favors benign forgetfulness.

stem: Lady in the 70s has type 2 DM on metformin 1 g BID had problems in naming and calling things lately.For example, she says animal instead of "cat" when she sees a cat. She has no memory impairment or personality changes. Her family is worried about her. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: problems in naming and calling things
no memory impairment or personality changes
why_right: The decisive clue is isolated naming difficulty with loss of word meaning (she says "animal" instead of "cat") while memory and personality are preserved. This is the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia (semantic dementia), which falls under the frontotemporal dementia spectrum. FTD presents with either a behavioral picture or a language picture, and the language variants spare episodic memory early.
why_wrong_block:
A. Vascular dementia: stepwise decline with focal deficits, stroke history and early executive dysfunction. Diabetes is a risk factor, but nothing focal or stepwise is described.
B. Alzheimer's dementia: starts with recent (episodic) memory loss; language problems come later. Here memory is explicitly normal.
D. B12 deficiency with cognitive features: metformin can lower B12, but deficiency gives global cognitive slowing or memory problems with neuropathy, ataxia or anemia, not an isolated loss of word meaning.
key_concept:
Dementia type is decided by the FIRST domain affected.
  • Recent memory first: Alzheimer
  • Behavior/disinhibition or language first, memory spared: frontotemporal
  • Stepwise, focal signs, executive dysfunction: vascular
  • Fluctuation, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism: Lewy body
  • Gait + incontinence + cognition: NPH
exam_pearl: Anomia with lost word meaning and normal memory points to FTD (semantic variant); do not let the metformin detail pull you to B12.

stem: Child was eating seeds and developed stridor, upon examination there was diminished air entry at right lung. (They gave a chext x-ray showing darker and hyperinflation of right lung)... it was obvious How to manage?
highlight_terms_source: diminished air entry at right lung
why_right: A child eating seeds who develops stridor with diminished air entry on the right and a CXR showing a hyperlucent, hyperinflated right lung (air trapping from a ball-valve obstruction) has an aspirated bronchial foreign body. When the diagnosis is this obvious, rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is both diagnostic and therapeutic and is the management of choice for removal.
why_wrong_block:
A. A lateral neck X-ray helps for croup (steeple sign), epiglottitis (thumb sign) or a radiopaque upper airway object; the foreign body here is bronchial, already shown on CXR, and seeds are radiolucent anyway.
B. Laryngoscopy visualizes only the larynx (used for laryngomalacia or laryngeal foreign bodies); it cannot reach or remove an object in the right main bronchus.
D. A tracheal procedure (for example tracheostomy) is reserved for an airway that cannot be secured otherwise; a stable child with a bronchial foreign body needs removal by rigid bronchoscopy.
key_concept:
Suspected airway foreign body in a child: rigid bronchoscopy.
  • Clues: choking episode, nuts/seeds, sudden unilateral wheeze or reduced air entry
  • CXR: ipsilateral hyperinflation (air trapping), mediastinal shift away; expiratory/decubitus films help
  • Most organic objects are radiolucent; a normal CXR does not exclude
  • Rigid bronchoscopy = diagnostic and therapeutic
exam_pearl: Unilateral hyperinflation after eating nuts or seeds means a ball-valve bronchial foreign body; go straight to rigid bronchoscopy.

stem: A family brought their kid who has fever, cough, and runny nose. Symptoms started after hx of choking after he ingested of some seed. Chest exam: dec RT side breathing sound. X ray pictures was shown . What is the next thing to do?
OptC: Send home with antipyretic and nasal fluid
highlight_terms_source: choking after he ingested of some seed
why_right: Fever, cough and coryza that started after a choking episode on seeds, with decreased right-sided breath sounds, point to a retained bronchial foreign body (often right-sided because the right main bronchus is more vertical), possibly with distal infection. The next step is bronchoscopy (rigid) to confirm and remove the object; the history of choking must not be dismissed as a simple viral illness.
why_wrong_block:
A. Subcutaneous epinephrine treats anaphylaxis (urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension); there is no allergic picture here, and adrenaline does not remove an obstructing object.
C. Sending home with antipyretics fits a simple URTI; a choking history plus unilateral reduced air entry is a foreign body until proven otherwise, and missing it leads to recurrent pneumonia or bronchiectasis.
key_concept:
Choking history + unilateral chest signs = foreign body until bronchoscopy says otherwise.
  • Right main bronchus is the commonest site
  • Late presentation: fever, cough, persistent or recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe
  • Management: rigid bronchoscopy
exam_pearl: Fever and cough do not cancel a choking history; unilateral signs after a seed still mean bronchoscopy.

stem: MVA , fractured 3 ribs Patient at first stable Then become distressed Chest clear , :
highlight_terms_source: at first stable Then become distressed
key_concept:
Deterioration after blunt chest trauma: match the sign to the lesion.
  • Paradoxical segment + multiple rib fractures: flail chest (supportive: analgesia, oxygen, ventilation)
  • Hypotension + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds + equal air entry: cardiac tamponade
  • Absent breath sounds + hyperresonance + tracheal shift: tension pneumothorax
  • Dull base + absent breath sounds: haemothorax
  • Delayed, progressive hypoxia with a clear chest on auscultation: pulmonary contusion
exam_pearl: Paradoxical movement means flail chest, raised JVP with hypotension and equal air entry means tamponade, and isolated progressive hypoxia means contusion: find the sign before naming the lesion.

stem: A 32-year-old healthy woman had neck ultrasound to evaluate lipoma; incidentally, there was right thyroid lobe 2.3 cm solid hypoechoic nodule (see lab results and report). Test Result Normal Values Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone 2.3 0.4-5.0 pU/mL. Thyroxine (T4 free serum) 11.3 8.5 - 15.2 pmol/L. Fine Needle Aspiration: Follicular neoplasm, Bethesda 4. Which of the following is most appropriate management?
why_right: The decisive clue is the FNA result "follicular neoplasm, Bethesda 4". Cytology cannot separate follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma because that needs capsular or vascular invasion on histology, so the lobe must be removed: hemithyroidectomy (diagnostic lobectomy). The normal TSH and free T4 confirm a non-functioning nodule, so no scan or antithyroid step is needed first.
why_wrong_block:
A. Nodule excision (enucleation) is not an oncological thyroid operation; it leaves uncertain margins and makes later completion surgery harder. Lobectomy is the minimum for a Bethesda 4 lesion.
C. Ultrasound surveillance suits a benign (Bethesda 2) nodule or a nodule below the FNA threshold; it is unsafe for an indeterminate lesion that may be follicular carcinoma.
D. Radiofrequency ablation is for cytologically benign, symptomatic nodules; it destroys tissue and gives no histology, so it is not used for possibly malignant lesions.
key_concept:
Bethesda category decides thyroid nodule management.
  • 1 Nondiagnostic: repeat FNA
  • 2 Benign: ultrasound follow-up
  • 3 AUS/FLUS: repeat FNA
  • 4 Follicular neoplasm: hemithyroidectomy
  • 5 Suspicious for malignancy: manage as 4 or 6
  • 6 Malignant: thyroidectomy (lobectomy or total by size and risk)
exam_pearl: Low TSH with a nodule goes to isotope scan first; normal TSH with Bethesda 4 goes straight to hemithyroidectomy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option B marked with ** and highlighted.

stem: RTA case with facial injuries Desaturating Next step?
key_concept:
Trauma airway ladder.
  • Intubation indications: SpO2 below 88%, GCS 8 or less, unconscious, aspiration risk
  • Indication + intact face: endotracheal intubation
  • Indication + major facial or mandibular injury: cricothyroidotomy
  • Nasal adjuncts and nasal tubes: avoid in midface or basal skull fracture
  • Tracheostomy: not the emergency choice in adults
exam_pearl: Facial injury moves the choice to a surgical airway only when it makes oral intubation unsafe or impossible (distorted anatomy, profuse oral bleeding); otherwise intubate.

stem: day 6/7 Post OP (appendectomy i think) fever ,dry wound
why_right: Fever on day 6 to 7 after surgery with a "dry wound" gives no local target: there is no discharge to culture and no collection to open. Among the options, the useful step is to review the drug chart, since drug fever (commonly from antibiotics) is a recognised cause of late postoperative fever when the wound and other sources look clean.
why_wrong_block:
A. A wound swab needs discharge; a dry wound gives nothing to culture. It is right when the wound is red, tender or discharging pus.
B. A throat swab has no role in postoperative fever without sore throat or pharyngitis symptoms.
C. Re-opening the wound treats a wound abscess or infected collection (pain, redness, swelling, pus); with a dry, quiet wound there is no indication.
key_concept:
Postoperative fever by day (the 5 W's).
  • Day 1: atelectasis (wind)
  • Days 2 to 3: pneumonia, UTI (water), superficial thrombophlebitis
  • Days 4 to 5: wound infection, DVT (walking)
  • Day 5 to 7 onward: intra-abdominal abscess, anastomotic leak
  • Any day: drugs (wonder drugs), lines
exam_pearl: After appendectomy a late fever with a clean wound still needs abdominal and DRE examination for a pelvic or intra-abdominal abscess.

stem: A 45-years old female in 5th day post-hysterectomy the patient have fever, she does not complain of anything (Literally Written) and the wound is clean. What is your next step of measurement?
why_right: This recall's key is medication review because the patient is on day 5 with fever but "does not complain of anything" and the "wound is clean": there are no urinary, chest or wound clues to direct tests. Drug fever is a non-invasive, often overlooked cause to check first in an asymptomatic postoperative patient.
why_wrong_block:
A. CBC and blood cultures are right when the patient looks septic (rigors, tachycardia, hypotension) or has a line or clear source; in a well, asymptomatic patient they are not the first step in this recall.
B. Urinalysis and culture is right for fever with urinary symptoms or a catheter, typically on days 2 to 3; here the patient has no complaints.
C. A chest X-ray is right for cough, dyspnoea, crackles or reduced breath sounds, mostly in the first days after surgery (atelectasis, pneumonia); there are no chest findings here.
key_concept:
Asymptomatic postoperative fever: start with the history, examination and drug chart before blind tests.
  • Day 1: atelectasis
  • Days 2 to 3: pneumonia, UTI, thrombophlebitis
  • Days 4 to 5: wound infection, DVT
  • After hysterectomy: also vaginal cuff cellulitis or pelvic collection
  • Drug fever: diagnosis of exclusion; patient often looks well
exam_pearl: Symptoms or signs pointing to a source (dysuria, cough, red wound) move the answer to the matching test.

stem: A man underwent a sigmoid resection, On postoperative day 4, he develops feve What Is MOST IMPORTANT Thing To Do? (or To Assess) (Not Next, Not Most Appropriate) (Don't Remember The Whole Case But It Was Short And No Exam Findings)
why_right: Fever on "postoperative day 4" falls in the window (days 4 to 5) when surgical site infection is the classic cause, and the lead-in asks for the most important thing to assess. Examining the wound is a bedside step that directly confirms or excludes the commonest cause before any test.
why_wrong_block:
A. A chest X-ray targets atelectasis or pneumonia, which cause fever on day 1 and days 2 to 3, or a patient with chest signs.
B. Blood cultures are right in a septic, unstable patient or with a central line; they come after clinical examination identifies the likely source.
D. Medication review fits a well patient with a clean wound and no source found; it is considered after the wound and abdomen are assessed.
key_concept:
Match the postoperative day to the likely source.
  • Day 1: atelectasis
  • Days 2 to 3: pneumonia, UTI, thrombophlebitis
  • Days 4 to 5: wound infection, DVT
  • After bowel resection, days 5 to 7: anastomotic leak, intra-abdominal abscess
exam_pearl: Day 4 fever: examine the wound first; day 1 to 3 fever: think chest and urine.

stem: 10 years old boy presented to the emergency department with fever, headache and sore throat for 2 days, in examination there were enlarged tonsils with exudate and pharyngeal petechiae. He had enlargement of anterior and posterior cervical lymph nodes. The rapid strep test was positive. BP: 100/65 T: 39 Others normal What's the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Fever, tonsillar exudate, pharyngeal petechiae and tender cervical nodes in a 10-year-old fit group A streptococcal pharyngitis, and the rapid strep test is positive, which confirms it. A positive rapid antigen test is acted on directly: start antibiotics, with oral penicillin V (or amoxicillin) for 10 days to prevent rheumatic fever.
why_wrong_block:
B. Throat culture is the back-up test when the rapid strep test is negative in a child with a suggestive picture; after a positive rapid test it only delays treatment.
C. Reassurance fits viral pharyngitis (mild hyperemia, coryza, cough, negative rapid test); confirmed GAS needs antibiotics to prevent rheumatic fever and suppurative complications.
D. This option was not recalled, so it cannot be judged; with a confirmed positive rapid test, antibiotic treatment remains the next step.
key_concept:
Pediatric sore throat with GAS features: test, then treat by result.
  • Rapid antigen test positive: treat (penicillin V or amoxicillin, 10 days)
  • Rapid test negative in a child: confirm with throat culture
  • Penicillin allergy: macrolide or cephalosporin depending on reaction type
  • Treating prevents rheumatic fever
exam_pearl: Culture is for the negative rapid test in children; a positive rapid test goes straight to penicillin.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-0131 → B. Throat culture. Confirm before the exam.

stem: down$ (didn't say down) depressed nasal bridge and Single Palmar Crease.
why_right: A depressed (flat) nasal bridge and single palmar crease are dysmorphic features of Down syndrome. The most common endocrine disorder in trisomy 21 is hypothyroidism (congenital or acquired, mostly autoimmune), which is why these children have repeated thyroid screening.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcaemia is the classic endocrine feature of DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome, not Down syndrome.
C. Hypopituitarism is not a characteristic association of trisomy 21; it goes with midline defects such as septo-optic dysplasia.
D. Hyperthyroidism (Graves) is more frequent in Down syndrome than in the general population but far less common than hypothyroidism.
key_concept:
Down syndrome: recognize the face, then screen the associations.
  • Features: upslanting eyes, epicanthic folds, Brushfield spots, flat nasal bridge, protruding tongue, single palmar crease, hypotonia
  • Heart: endocardial cushion (AVSD) defect most typical
  • Endocrine: hypothyroidism most common
  • Also: duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung, leukaemia, atlantoaxial instability, early Alzheimer
exam_pearl: Hypoparathyroidism is the DiGeorge trap; Down syndrome = hypothyroid.

stem: A 4-month-old boy with down syndrome exhibits poor weight gain, tachypnea, a low-pitched grade 2 systolic murmur and a fixed splitting of S2. Chest X-ray reveals cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascularity. Electrocardiography documents biventricular hypertrophy and a superior frontal plane QRS axis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: An infant with Down syndrome, failure to thrive, tachypnea, cardiomegaly and plethoric lungs has a large left to right shunt. The fixed splitting of S2 points to an atrial level component, biventricular hypertrophy means both atrial and ventricular shunting, and a superior frontal QRS axis is the ECG hallmark of AVSD, the classic Down syndrome lesion.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coarctation gives upper limb hypertension with weak or delayed femoral pulses and is linked to Turner syndrome; it does not cause fixed split S2, plethoric lungs or a superior axis.
B. PDA gives a continuous machinery murmur with bounding pulses; S2 is not fixed split and the axis is not superior. Think PDA in prematurity or congenital rubella.
C. An isolated VSD gives a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border without fixed S2 splitting or a superior axis. It is the second most common lesion in Down syndrome.
key_concept:
Down syndrome + fixed split S2 + superior (left) QRS axis = AVSD (endocardial cushion defect).
  • Down: AVSD, then VSD
  • Turner: coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve
  • Fixed split S2: atrial level shunt (ASD or AVSD)
  • Superior axis on ECG: AVSD (also primum ASD)
  • Large shunt: cardiomegaly, plethora, early heart failure
exam_pearl: Fixed split S2 with a NORMAL or right axis suggests secundum ASD; a SUPERIOR axis in Down syndrome flips it to AVSD.

stem: In which of the following conditions would you expect a bone age greater than the chronologic age?
why_right: The question asks where bone age exceeds chronological age. In congenital adrenal hyperplasia excess adrenal androgens accelerate epiphyseal maturation, so bone age runs ahead. These children are tall early but fuse early, ending with short adult height.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hypothyroidism: thyroid hormone is needed for skeletal maturation, so bone age is markedly delayed.
B. Chronic renal failure: chronic illness slows growth and delays bone age.
C. Familial short stature: bone age equals chronological age; the child is simply following short parents.
key_concept:
Sex steroid excess advances bone age; most growth failure delays it.
  • Advanced: CAH, precocious puberty, obesity, exogenous sex steroids
  • Delayed: hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, chronic illness (CKD, IBD), constitutional delay
  • Normal: familial short stature
  • CAH: commonest cause 21 hydroxylase deficiency; raised 17 hydroxyprogesterone
exam_pearl: Tall child now but short adult = advanced bone age from androgens or estrogens.

stem: Which of the following syndromes is associated with coarctation of the aorta?
why_right: Turner syndrome (45,X) is the syndrome classically linked to coarctation of the aorta, along with bicuspid aortic valve. A short girl with upper limb hypertension and weak femoral pulses should prompt karyotype for Turner.
why_wrong_block:
A. Down syndrome is associated with AVSD (endocardial cushion defect), then VSD; coarctation is not its signature lesion.
C. Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) is mainly associated with VSD and PDA, with overlapping fingers and rocker bottom feet.
D. Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) is mainly associated with VSD, ASD and PDA, with midline defects such as cleft lip and palate.
key_concept:
Syndrome to heart lesion pairs:
  • Turner: coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve
  • Down: AVSD, VSD
  • Edwards (T18): VSD, PDA
  • Patau (T13): VSD, ASD, PDA
  • Williams: supravalvular aortic stenosis
  • Noonan: pulmonary valve stenosis
exam_pearl: Turner = coarctation, but Noonan (normal karyotype, similar look) = pulmonary stenosis; do not mix them up.

stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with a 1-day history of abdominal pain and vomiting. He was afebrile and has no diarrhea. He has bilateral knee pain, and there was some tenderness of the knee joints, but no effusions. Within 24 hours, he developed a rash on his legs and buttocks, which is petechial and purpuric, and his platelet count was normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: rash on his legs and buttocks
why_right: A 4-year-old with abdominal pain and vomiting, bilateral knee pain without effusion, then a petechial and purpuric rash on the legs and buttocks with a normal platelet count is the classic picture of HSP (IgA vasculitis). The purpura is vasculitic, not thrombocytopenic, and GI symptoms may precede the rash.
why_wrong_block:
A. SLE is rare at age 4, usually affects adolescent girls, and tends to cause malar rash and cytopenias, not dependent purpura with normal platelets.
B. HUS follows bloody diarrhea and causes hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury; here there is no diarrhea and platelets are normal.
D. Kawasaki disease needs fever for 5 days or more with conjunctivitis, mucosal and extremity changes and lymphadenopathy; this child is afebrile.
key_concept:
HSP = purpura with normal platelets + arthralgia + abdominal pain + renal involvement.
  • Typical age: about 3 to 10 years, often after URTI
  • Rash: palpable purpura on legs and buttocks
  • Platelets and coagulation: normal
  • GI risk: intussusception
  • Follow up: urine and BP for nephritis
exam_pearl: Purpura with LOW platelets points to ITP, HUS or leukemia; purpura with NORMAL platelets on the legs and buttocks points to HSP.

stem: A 6-month-old infant with cough and fever diagnosed as bronchiolitis. On examination, she had mild distress with intercostal retraction and chest auscultation reveals diffuse crackles. Blood pressure 92/67 mmHg, Heart rate 145 /min, Respiratory rate 56 /min, Temperature 36.6 °C, Oxygen saturation 89 %. Which of the following is the best management?
OptA: Admit for oxygen and hydration therapy
OptB: Send home with instruction when to come back
OptC: Admit for antibiotics and oxygen administration
OptD: Admit for bronchodilation and steroid management
why_right: Bronchiolitis is viral and managed supportively. This infant has SpO2 89%, RR 56 and intercostal retractions, so she is hypoxic and needs admission for supplemental oxygen and fluid support (feeding is often impaired by tachypnea).
why_wrong_block:
B. Discharge is safe only for a well infant feeding adequately with normal saturation; hypoxia and tachypnea make it unsafe here.
C. Bronchiolitis is viral (mostly RSV); antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of secondary bacterial infection. Crackles are expected in bronchiolitis and do not mean pneumonia.
D. Bronchodilators and steroids are not routinely recommended in bronchiolitis because they do not improve outcomes; they belong to asthma management.
key_concept:
Bronchiolitis = supportive care: oxygen if hypoxic + hydration/feeding support.
  • Cause: RSV most common, under 2 years
  • Clinical diagnosis; CXR not routine
  • Admit: hypoxia, significant distress, poor feeding, apnea, very young age
  • Not routine: antibiotics, bronchodilators, steroids
exam_pearl: Same infant with normal saturation and good feeding goes home with return precautions; low saturation flips the answer to admission.

stem: A 78-year-old man presents with 2-year history of slow and progressive deterioration in his memory. The patient is able to perform some activities of daily living, including dressing and bathing. His personality has changed from that of a kind and caring person into someone who has periods of agitation and aggression. Neurologic and musculoskeletal examination cannot be carried out. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: 2-year history of slow and progressive deterioration in his memory
why_right: A 78-year-old with a 2-year slow, progressive decline that starts with memory fits Alzheimer's disease, the most common dementia. Personality change with agitation and aggression appears as the disease advances, and the gradual (not stepwise) course with no vascular history supports it.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mixed dementia: needs evidence of both Alzheimer and cerebrovascular disease (strokes, stepwise decline, imaging changes); nothing vascular is given.
C. Multi-infarct dementia: stepwise deterioration with focal neurological signs and vascular risk factors; here the course is smooth and slow.
D. Major depressive disorder: can mimic dementia (pseudodementia) but has prominent low mood, anhedonia and subacute onset; it does not cause a steady 2-year memory decline with aggression.
key_concept:
Alzheimer = insidious, gradually progressive, memory first.
  • Early: recent memory loss
  • Later: language, visuospatial, personality change, agitation
  • Stepwise + focal signs: think vascular
  • Mood symptoms leading the picture: think depression
exam_pearl: Smooth progressive decline beginning with memory is Alzheimer; a stepwise course would flip it to vascular.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Department with epigastric pain for 6-days, radiating to the back, associated with frequent vomiting. She is known to have multiple small gallstones. Physical examination confirmed diffuse abdominal distention, epigastric tenderness with sluggish bowel sounds (see lab results and report). Test Result Normal Values: Alkaline phosphatase 115 39-117 IU/L; Amylase 149 24-151 IU/L; Direct bilirubin 5.6 1.5-6.5 mol/L; Total bilirubin 15.8 3.5-16.5 mol/L. Erect chest X-ray: Left pleural effusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?
highlight_terms_source: epigastric pain for 6-days, radiating to the back
why_right: This recall's key is urine amylase. Pain for "6 days" radiating to the back, gallstones, ileus (distension, sluggish bowel sounds) and a left pleural effusion suggest acute pancreatitis, but serum amylase (149) is already normal because it falls back within a few days. Urinary amylase stays raised longer, so it is the key's way to confirm a late-presenting pancreatitis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Trans-abdominal ultrasound is the initial imaging in acute pancreatitis to look for gallstones; the key rejects it here because the question targets biochemical confirmation of a late presentation with normal serum amylase.
C. CT is reserved for an unclear diagnosis or for severity and complications, ideally after 48 to 72 hours; it is not the initial investigation.
D. Analysis of aspirated gastrointestinal fluid has no diagnostic role in acute pancreatitis.
key_concept:
Acute pancreatitis needs 2 of 3: typical pain, enzymes above 3 times normal, typical imaging.
  • Serum amylase normalises within days; lipase and urinary amylase stay raised longer
  • Ultrasound: look for gallstones (biliary cause)
  • CT: unclear diagnosis or complications, after 48 to 72 hours
  • Left pleural effusion and sentinel loop/ileus support pancreatitis
exam_pearl: A late presenter with normal serum amylase does not exclude pancreatitis; pick the test that stays elevated longer.

stem: A 45-year-old diabetic man underwent a laparotomy for a diverticular perforation. On the 4th post-operative day, he developed a high-grade fever with chills and multiple spikes. On examination, his wound is healthy and his chest is clear to auscultation. On Digital rectal examination, there is bogginess anteriorly. Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate 120 /min, Respiratory rate 18 /min, Temperature 38 °C. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
highlight_terms_source: high-grade fever with chills and multiple spikes
why_right: High spiking fever with chills on "day 4" after laparotomy for a perforated diverticulum, with a healthy wound and clear chest, removes wound and chest causes. "Bogginess anteriorly" on DRE localises a pelvic abscess. An established abscess must be drained, so image-guided drainage (with antibiotics as an adjunct) is the treatment.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV antibiotics alone do not clear an established abscess; they are an adjunct to drainage and suit only small collections (under about 4 cm).
B. IV paracetamol only lowers the temperature and does nothing for the pelvic abscess.
C. Abdominal washout (relaparotomy) is for generalised peritonitis, multiple collections, an unstable patient or failed percutaneous drainage; this is a localised collection.
key_concept:
Postoperative intra-abdominal collection: size and stability decide.
  • Small collection: antibiotics
  • Collection of about 4 x 4 cm or more: percutaneous image-guided drainage
  • Multiple collections: laparoscopy
  • Unstable patient or peritonitis: laparotomy
  • Anterior rectal bogginess on DRE = pelvic abscess
exam_pearl: Spiking fever with a clean wound and clear chest after abdominal surgery: do a DRE and look for a pelvic abscess.

stem: A 50-year-old patient underwent a total thyroidectomy 5 hours ago. He has developed a large neck swelling associated with stridor and shortness of breath. Blood pressure 165/90 mmHg, Heart rate 130 /min, Respiratory rate 24 /min, Temperature 37 °C. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: A "large neck swelling" with "stridor and shortness of breath" only "5 hours" after total thyroidectomy is a compressive haematoma. The treatment that relieves the airway fastest is opening the skin and strap muscle sutures at the bedside to evacuate the clot, then returning to theatre to control bleeding.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tracheostomy does not remove the compressing clot and is slow through a swollen, distorted neck; evacuation of the haematoma comes first.
B. Close observation is dangerous with stridor; a tense haematoma can obstruct the airway within minutes.
C. Percutaneous drainage fails because a haematoma is clotted blood, and it delays decompression.
key_concept:
Early complications after thyroidectomy.
  • Hours: neck swelling + stridor = haematoma: bedside wound opening
  • Hoarseness, aspiration: recurrent laryngeal nerve
  • Loss of high-pitched voice: superior laryngeal nerve
  • Perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm: hypocalcaemia (check calcium)
  • Refractory hypocalcaemia: check magnesium
exam_pearl: Swelling plus stridor within hours of thyroid surgery means open the wound now, not intubate or scan first.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe abdominal pain and absolute constipation for 2 days associated with nausea and vomiting. He has a significant past history of constipation requiring use of laxatives. On examination, his abdomen is distended, tense, tender all over with a palpable mass in the left lumbar and hypochondrium (see image). Which of the following is the most likely site of volvulus?
why_right: Pain, "absolute constipation" and vomiting with a distended tense abdomen mean large bowel obstruction. The "long history of constipation requiring laxatives" (elongated, redundant sigmoid) and a "mass in the left lumbar and hypochondrium" (the twisted, dilated loop) point to sigmoid volvulus, the commonest colonic volvulus.
why_wrong_block:
A. Caecal volvulus occurs in younger patients with a congenitally mobile caecum, without the long laxative history; the dilated caecum often moves toward the epigastrium or left upper abdomen with small bowel dilatation, so the chronic constipation is the decisive clue against it.
B. The rectum is fixed in the pelvis without a mobile mesentery, so it does not twist.
D. Transverse colon volvulus is very rare and would give a central or upper abdominal mass rather than a left-sided mass with chronic constipation.
key_concept:
Colonic volvulus: site by clue.
  • Sigmoid: elderly, chronic constipation, laxatives, institutionalised; left-sided mass; coffee bean loop pointing to RUQ
  • Caecum: younger, mobile caecum; dilated caecum displaced toward LUQ or epigastrium, small bowel dilated
  • Stable sigmoid volvulus: endoscopic (sigmoidoscopic) decompression
  • Ischaemia, perforation or peritonitis: sigmoid colectomy with end colostomy
exam_pearl: Chronic constipation on laxatives in an older patient is the clue for sigmoid; a twisted caecum can also end up on the left, so the side of the mass alone can mislead.

stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C and liver cirrhosis presented to Emergency Room with perforated peptic ulcer that requires urgent laparotomy (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values: Hb 90 130-170 g/L (Male) - 120-160 g/L (Female); Platelets count 90 150-400 x 109/L; INR 2 0.8-1.2; Prothrombin time 17 10-13 sec. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management prior to the procedure?
why_right: This cirrhotic patient needs an urgent laparotomy and his main correctable defect is the coagulopathy: INR 2 and PT 17 reflect poor hepatic synthesis of clotting factors. Fresh frozen plasma replaces the whole range of clotting factors, so it is the most appropriate product to give before the procedure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Platelets: the count of 90 is low but well above the level usually needed for major surgery (around 50); platelets are given when the count is below that or there is platelet dysfunction.
B. Cryoprecipitate: mainly supplies fibrinogen (plus factor VIII and vWF); it is right for low fibrinogen or DIC, not for a raised INR from global factor deficiency.
D. Packed red blood cells: Hb 90 is above the usual restrictive threshold of 70 in a stable patient and does not correct bleeding risk; give RBCs for active major bleeding or Hb below threshold.
key_concept:
Match the blood product to the defect.
  • High PT/INR (factor deficiency, cirrhosis, urgent surgery): FFP
  • Warfarin reversal with bleeding: vitamin K IV plus PCC or FFP
  • Low fibrinogen / DIC: cryoprecipitate
  • Low platelets for major surgery or bleeding: platelets
  • Low Hb or active hemorrhage: packed RBCs
exam_pearl: In cirrhosis the abnormal number to fix before urgent surgery is the INR, not a mildly low platelet count or Hb.

stem: A 65-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of vague upper abdominal pain associated with progressive yellowish discoloration of his sclera, dark urine and weight loss. On examination, he was jaundiced with a palpable, distended non-tender gallbladder (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values: Alkaline phosphatase 320 39-117 IU/L; Direct bilirubin 77 1.5-6.5 mol/L; Total bilirubin 88 3.5-16.5 mol/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Progressive jaundice with only vague pain, dark urine and weight loss over 3 months in a 65-year-old point to malignant obstruction. A palpable, distended, non-tender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) means the block is distal to the cystic duct junction, which is the territory of a periampullary tumour (pancreatic head, ampulla, distal CBD, duodenum).
why_wrong_block:
A. Klatskin tumour: obstructs at the hilum above the cystic duct, so the gallbladder is collapsed and not palpable; right when US shows only intrahepatic dilatation with a shrunken gallbladder.
C. Common bile duct stone: the gallbladder is usually chronically inflamed and fibrosed so it does not distend, and jaundice tends to fluctuate with pain; right in fluctuating jaundice with biliary colic or cholangitis.
D. Hepatocellular carcinoma: causes a hepatocellular or mixed picture in a cirrhotic liver, not a distended gallbladder; think of it with cirrhosis, hepatomegaly and raised AFP.
key_concept:
Gallbladder state localises the biliary block.
  • Distended, non-tender, palpable (Courvoisier): distal block, periampullary or pancreatic head cancer
  • Collapsed gallbladder with intrahepatic dilatation only: hilar block, Klatskin tumour
  • Fluctuating jaundice with colic: CBD stone
  • Weight loss plus progressive jaundice: malignancy until proven otherwise
exam_pearl: Courvoisier sign = jaundice + palpable non-tender gallbladder, which is unlikely to be stones.

stem: A 67-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of yellowish discoloration of his sclera and skin with dark urine and pale stool. On examination, he was jaundiced with a palpable distended gallbladder (see report and lab results). Test Result Normal Values: Alkaline phosphatase 421 39-117 IU/L; Direct bilirubin 122.3 1.5-6.5 mol/L; Total bilirubin 134.5 3.5-16.5 umol/L. Ultrasound: Dilated intra and extrahepatic bile ducts with hugely distended gallbladder. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Dilated intra and extrahepatic bile ducts with hugely distended gallbladder
why_right: Jaundice with dark urine and pale stool plus very high ALP and direct bilirubin is obstructive jaundice. The palpable distended gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) and US showing dilated intra- AND extrahepatic ducts with a hugely distended gallbladder put the block at the distal CBD, classically from pancreatic head cancer in an older man.
why_wrong_block:
A. Klatskin tumour: a hilar block gives intrahepatic dilatation only with a collapsed gallbladder; here the extrahepatic ducts and gallbladder are distended.
C. Mirizzi's syndrome: a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck compresses the common hepatic duct, usually with a contracted, inflamed gallbladder and pain; right in a gallstone patient with dilatation above the cystic duct level only.
D. Common bile duct stone: can dilate both duct systems, but the scarred stone-bearing gallbladder rarely distends and jaundice is usually painful and fluctuating.
key_concept:
Level of obstruction on US.
  • Intra + extrahepatic dilatation, big gallbladder: distal CBD, pancreatic head / periampullary tumour
  • Intrahepatic only, collapsed gallbladder: hilum, Klatskin tumour
  • Gallbladder neck stone compressing CHD: Mirizzi syndrome
exam_pearl: A hugely distended gallbladder with painless obstructive jaundice argues against stones and for a distal malignancy.
